Show friend markers - Shows the locations of all active friends Show previous jumps - Tracks all prior waypoint systems along your current route. Show navigation markers - Displays scheduled route markers.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_factions_descr: The Factions tab lists the names of all factions active within the system.
The information provided for each faction is:

- The faction’s superpower allegiance - The faction’s government type - The faction’s Influence. This shows how powerful the faction is within the system and is primarily increased or decreased via combat, missions or trade involving system factions. - Any State affecting the faction. - Your current reputation with the faction.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_featplaninfo_d: The Services and Planetary Information tabs are available contextually depending on the selected target. A port will show the Services tab, listing all available services at that location:

- Docking, for landing pad access. - Contacts, for a variety of contacts offering voucher exchanges and bounty claims, among other things. - Exploration, indicating a Universal Cartographics office is present. - Concourse, for a range of vendors useful for surface activities. See the Concourse guide for more information. - Refuel, for ship refuelling options. - Repair, for ship repair options. - Restock, for restocking all ammunition stores and vehicle hangars/bays. - Outfitting, for the trade, installation and storage of ship modules and hardpoints. - Shipyard, for the trade, transfer and storage of ships. - Crew Lounge, for the hiring and management of crew members. - AUTO DOCK, for locations where automated docking procedures are accepted. - POWER CONTACT, for Powerplay collections and contributions. - Search and Rescue, for handing in commodities related to missing or vulnerable people. - Services, indicating that a local service interface is available. - Missions, for an active mission contract board. - Livery, for the visual customisation of ships and other extras.

Ports will also provide a summary of their main imports and exports, along with goods prohibited at this location. The latter is determined by the faction operating the power, while the imports and exports relate to the port’s primary economy type and active state.
An astronomical body shows the Planetary Information tab, which details scientific information about its composition and local features.

Most importantly this includes whether an atmosphere is present, the composition of the body and the Locations tally. Locations are known areas on a planet with structures built by a particular civilisation. Human locations are common throughout inhabited space, but Guardian and Thargoid structures are also found in some systems.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_interface_desc: The map interface consists of two tabs columns. To the left are the Map Display tabs, while the right provides Map Target tabs when a star system or object has been targeted. Each of these tabs will be discussed in the following pages.

Route Itinerary The itinerary of a plotted route will be displayed at the bottom of the map interface. This includes your current location, the next system waypoint and estimated jumps remaining, and the set destination.
Search Function The galaxy map also offers a search bar for finding stars, planets and starports by name. Selecting a result will move your map cursor to it.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_introduction_d: The Maps interface – encompassing the galaxy, system and planetary maps – is the primary method of navigation through the stars. Detailed information is provided about every star system in the galaxy, along with the worlds, factions and unique features that populate them. These maps can be extensively filtered as needed to highlight specific information or search results.
For Commanders, the map also displays icons of specific interest to them. This includes navigation and mission markers, the location of friends and teammates, bookmarked locations and much more.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_mapmode_descri: Map Mode provides a sub-list display and filter options for the galaxy map. Each of these options can be adjusted to isolate star systems as desired.

Allegiance - Shows systems by the superpower allegiance of the governing faction with, if any. Civilisation - Shows systems inhabited by humans, or those with a known Thargoid or Guardian presence. Government - Displays systems by the ruling government type. This can change as factions compete for dominance. The type of government impacts which goods are considered illegal in the system. Economy - Displays systems by primary economy type. Useful for traders, or pilots looking to outfit ships for a particular profession. State - Displays systems by active state, which is often influenced by pilot actions in the area. Some scenarios, such as conflict zones, are only available in certain states. Security - Shows systems by security level. Helpful for pilots seeking to avoid – or perhaps hide in – lawless systems. Star class - Displays systems by star class. This is of particular interest to pilots seeking to keep their fuel tanks filled on long journeys, or those seeking out neutron star boosts.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_mapview_descri: The Map View tab displays all astronomical bodies, starports and other objects in a system side by side.
This view provides the system’s makeup at a glance, ordered by each object’s distance from its star.  It lacks representation of the true distance between individual objects, however.
Bodies that can be landed on are ringed in blue. Bodies with a planetary port are additionally identified by three blue lines.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_marketinfo_des: The Market Information tab allows you to select a commodity to see where and for what price it is being traded in a system, depending on the active trade data you possess.
If more than one market is present in a system, they can be cycled through individually.
The Plot Route icon will select the currently highlighted market as your destination, rather than the system’s nav beacon.
The Compare Market icon toggles the highlighted market as the price comparison when viewing the commodities market.
Three additional filter toggles are provided when reviewing a system’s known market information:

- Show markets with large landing pads only.
- Show or exclude planetary markets.
- Show markets at all ranges, or choose between long/medium/short range markets.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_missions_descr: MY ACTIVE MISSIONS The My Active Missions tab displays all of your current mission contracts, including the location and distance from your current position. Selecting an entry will set it as your target.
SYSTEM MISSIONS With a system selected, the System Missions tab will appear in the Map Target list. This shows missions that are located at the currently selected target only.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_myfleet_descri: MY FLEET The My Fleet tab displays all ships you currently own. This includes their model, custom names, location and distance from your current position. Selecting an entry will set it as your target. The number beside the icon represents your fleet size.

STORED SHIPS With a system or market selected, the Stored Ships tab will appear in the Map Target list. This shows ships located at the currently selected target only, with that number displayed next to the icon.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_organicinfo_de: The Organic Information tab list all indexed flora and fauna on a system.
Different organic species will populate this tab once the target planet has been mapped with the Detailed Surface Scanner. Each species can be selected to highlight its presence on a planet.
While tenuous atmosphere planets can sustain organic life, not all such planets have organics on them.

Entries will have a First Reported By tag if another Commander has already logged organic data for that species on the selected planet. By being the first to hand in organic data for a planet, your name will be registered beside an entry.
The Organic Information tab is available when viewing a planetary map.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_orreryview_des: The Orrery View tab displays a virtual representation of the star system, including the orbital trajectory of all astronomical bodies and their relative distances from each other.
As with the system map, bodies that can be landed on are highlighted by a blue ring. Bodies with a planetary port are additionally identified by three blue lines.

In the orrery view, a + symbol to the left of a body indicates that there is more than one body at that location. Zooming in closer will reveal these bodies, which are often comprised of multiple satellites around a larger body.
Map cursor navigation uses the same approach as the galaxy map.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_pointsofintere: The Points of Interest tab lists all objects within a system that are of note to a Commander. Selecting an entry will set it as your target.
Points of interest are listed in the following categories:

Orbital Ports - Includes all known starports and outposts in the system Landfall Planets - All bodies can be approached with a Planetary Approach Suite. Note that bodies with a tenuous atmosphere require the Advanced Planetary Approach Suite module. Planetary Ports - Includes all known planetary ports in the system. Surface Settlements - Displays all known surface settlements explorable with the SRV. Odyssey Settlements - Displays all known surface settlements accessible with the Odyssey expansion. Fleet Carriers - Displays all fleet carriers stationed in the system.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_population_des: The Population Range tab offers an additional filter to a Map mode or User Data Mode overlay. You can choose to display systems that have a resident population within the set slider range.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_powerplayinfo_: The Powerplay Information tab provides an overview of a selected system’s Powerplay details.
Powerplay information screens will contain information about the Powerplay status of a selected system, including Powerplay state, control score bar and ethos activities for your power.
With a controlled system selected, system strength and beyond frontline penalties will be displayed along with the undermining and reinforcement scores for this cycle.
With a non-control system selected only the top two contesting Powers will be displayed alongside your own power if they are not in the top two.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_powerplaymode_: Powerplay Mode displays the current state of an ongoing struggle for dominance across inhabited space by agents pledged to a specific Power.

Full information on the Powerplay system is found on the help overlay in the Powerplay Overview screen of any power. The Powerplay menu, accessible from the Home screen of the Internal cockpit interface, provides the list of powers. Below is a summary of the information provided in the galaxy map interface.

MAP MODE: POWERPLAY Selecting a Power from the list will turn the filtering for them on or off. Toggle All Powers will toggle all Power options on or off based on the current majority filtering, if more Powers are filtered out then this option will filter all Powers out and vice versa.

Powers This section allows for the filtering of Powers, selecting one will toggle their filtering. This allows players to view the territory of specific Powers together or view all Powers at once. Hovering a Power will give a brief summery of the number of systems controlled by them and how many are in each control state.

Powerplay State This section allows for toggling system display by control state. This can be combined with toggling of Powers to create bespoke filters for finding systems in specific control states belonging to a selection of Powers.
MAP MODE: POWERPLAY ACTIVITY FILTER Choosing a Power from the drop-down list allows you to use the following options to filters via activity type and level.

Activity Type Selecting one of the options in this section allows you to filter for specific activity types, this will then display only the systems where the selected Power is capable of engaging in that activity.

Minimum Activity Level This can be toggled on to allow for filtering the activity type selected by the amount of activity that has been recently observed in the relevant systems. The higher the level filtered for the less systems will be shown as only the systems with large amounts of activity will be viable for the filter
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_precis: A guide to reading the maps that chart the galaxy.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_realisticmode_: With the Realistic display, star systems appear in the galaxy map as they would in the night sky. All systems will be displayed, as systems cannot be filtered in this mode. Map icons such as mission markers, bookmarks and ship locations will still appear.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_routesettings_: The Route Settings tab allows you to set custom parameters for route planning.
Route - Shows your current and destination systems. Selecting an entry will focus the map camera on it.
Jump data - Offers a choice between two route planning types:

<font color='#f8f8f8'>Economical</font>, the most efficient route for conserving fuel, containing more jumps.
<font color='#f8f8f8'>Fastest</font>, the fewest jumps between your current and target locations, spending more fuel with each jump.

If you wish to take advantage of neutron star boosts - while overcoming the inherent risks contained by doing so - you can also tell your ship computer to account for neutron stars along the route.

The FSD Boost toggle will show you how far you can travel using synthesis to boost your FSD for a single jump. Set the bar to the level of FSD boost you intend to use.

Cargo mass - Allows you to simulate how far you can travel with or without cargo. Put simply, the more a ship weighs the shorter its jump distance will be. Simply drag the cargo slider to the desired weight and plot a new route.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_systemcolonisa: The system map highlights active construction projects in the system, showing where commanders can deliver resources to help complete facilities. These construction sites will pay above the galactic average for delivered resources and when completed will provide benefits for the system.

Using the Architect view mode in the system map shows the locations where facilities can be placed and in progress construction projects. Information about ongoing projects, including the goods required to complete them, is also found here.
The system architect can use this view mode to select a construction site and choose a facility to build.
This map mode allows commanders to see available locations within range for System Colonisation. The mode will show which systems can and cannot be expanded into and why.
If System data is available, it will highlight the number of orbital and planetary construction sites. System data is not required to make a claim.
Data can be acquired by travelling to the system and using the FSS, see Pilot's handbook for more information on using the FSS.
Claimable systems must be uninhabited and within range of the system to be expanded from.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_systeminfo_des: The Route Settings tab allows you to set custom parameters for route planning.
Every system has a name and, if available, a description. The following information is also listed:

Allegiance - Shows the superpower this system is aligned with, if any. Population - The current resident population of the system. Only inhabited systems will have governments or economies. Government - The type of government currently in control of the system. This can change over time, as minor factions of different governments compete for dominance of a system. The government type influences which goods are considered illegal. Anarchy systems have no system security present. State - The current active state of a system, most often a result of recent activity. States impact the economy, security level, standard of living and missions types available in a system. For mercenaries looking for a fight, systems with a War or Civil War state contain active conflict zones to participate in. Economy - Lists the economy of a populated system, which dictates the type of goods imported and exported here. There can be more than one economy in a system. Security level - The current security level of the system. High security systems enjoy an increased authority presence, while low security systems attract pirates and scavengers. Anarchy systems lack an authority presence altogether and standard laws are typically ignored. Star type - The type of star considered the primary star of the system, based on the Morgan-Keenan classification system. Stars that can be scooped for fuel are one of the following types: O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Distance - The distance in light years from your current position. (Galaxy map only) Star class - The class of the star considered the primary star of the system. This includes neutron stars and black holes.
When in the System Map view, information about the controlling faction is also provided here.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_traderoutes_de: The Trade Routes displayed trending trade route data, based on the last 24 hours of activity.

The <font color='#f8f8f8'>Commanders</font> option shows trade activity by Commanders only, while <font color='#f8f8f8'>Commercial</font> displays information about general galactic trade by commercial pilots. <font color='#f8f8f8'>All</font> utilises both of these sources.
You can filter trade routes by type or by individual goods as needed.

BUY TRENDING TRADE DATA With a star system selected, the Map Target list offers a Buy Trending Trade Data tab. This is used to purchase trade data to populate trending trade route information for that system.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_userdatamode_d: User Data Mode provides a sub-list of categories that set the galaxy map to display results drawn from data you have collected or purchased. Systems excluded by the chosen filter cannot be selected with the map cursor
Services - Displays systems with specialised services present, such as material traders or black market contacts.
Visited stars - Allows a pilot to review which systems they have already visited, and which have yet to be seen.
Cartographic data - Highlights which nearby systems have cartographic data available for purchase.
Trade data - Highlights which nearby systems have trade data available for purchase, along with systems you have already acquired data for.
Commodity - This mode allows you to isolate systems that contain a market which imports or export a selected commodity.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_viewplanetarym: The View Planetary Map tab brings up a digital simulation of the selected planet, providing you have acquired data from a scan or data purchase.
All known surface locations are provided on the planetary map. These are selected in the same way as starport or astronomical bodies provide similar information or market data where applicable.

Additional points of interest will appear when a planet has been mapped, or when close enough for your sensors to sweep the planet’s surface. These surface points of interest often contain goods, data and other useful items used for trade, engineering and equipment upgrades. But be careful: other operatives are interested in the same rewards, and are unlikely to welcome competitors.
codex_pilotshandbook_maps_viewsystemmap_: The View System Map tab opens the map for the currently selected system. This provides a variety of new display options related to the contents of a system. Some tabs unique to the system map are provided, which are detailed in the following pages.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_advequipa: Increases the ship's hull integrity and resistance to damage.
Protects modules against weapons fire that penetrates the hull.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_advequips: Strengthens a ship's active shield when powered. Multiple boosters stack in effectiveness.
Regenerates a ship's active shield rapidly when triggered. Does not reboot a collapsed shield, and generates significant heat while powering up for use.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_advequipu: Fires chaff, which causes gimballed and turreted weaponry to lose lock on a ship. Requires ammunition.
Missile and torpedo defence. When deployed, causes affected ordnance to lose lock.
Tracks and fires upon any missiles, torpedoes in range when powered.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_advflight: Flight assist is an onboard computer that restricts flight parameters, simulating how a ship behaves when flown in an atmosphere. This makes the ship easier to operate for pilots unfamiliar with the physics of flight in zero gravity.

The default setting is flight assist on. However, some pilots opt to deactivate flight assist during combat, in order to increase a ship's turn rate. Flight assist can be toggled on and off via the control options.
When flight assist is deactivated, the speed and rotation of a vessel are dependent on the pilot manually employing thrust and counter-thrust to maintain control.
Although flying becomes less intuitive, deactivation of flight assist grants pilots the ability to perform advanced manoeuvres that can achieve superiority during combat.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_basiccomb: To use a weapon or module, it must be assigned to a fire group. Fire groups allow fast movement between customised hardpoint configurations. For example, one fire group may be set to deploy weapons, while another fire group operates scanners. You can select the next fire group using $BINDING_input_either:#value=CYCLEFIREGROUPNEXT;.

Hardpoints can be assigned to either primary or secondary fire. This allows each fire group to have two triggers.

For example, a fire group may be configured so that a ship's beam weapons are fired with the primary trigger, while missiles are launched with the secondary trigger.

Some combat-related modules set in utility mounts, such as scanners and chaff launchers, can also be assigned to primary or secondary fire.
All ships have a number of hardpoints, which are mounting positions on the hull for weapons and modules. Hardpoints come in four sizes:

• Class 1 – Small
• Class 2 – Medium
• Class 3 – Large
• Class 4 – Huge

Alongside hardpoints, all ships contain a number of utility mounts. These can be used to install additional devices, such as scanners and chaff launchers.
Weapons can be one of three different types:

• Fixed: The weapon fires straight forward with minimal target tracking. Fixed weapons generally do the most damage and are unaffected by chaff. • Gimbal: The weapon has limited movement and is able to track targets within a limited arc, increasing accuracy. Gimballed weapons offer standard damage output but can be countered with chaff. • Turret: The weapon has full rotational movement and tracks targets autonomously, with predetermined settings available in the Functions menu. Turreted weapons have the lowest damage output and can be countered with chaff.

When a hardpoint is deployed, it emerges from a compartment within the ship's hull in preparation for use. When a hardpoint is retracted, it is withdrawn back into the compartment.
Deployed weapons and modules provide a targeting reticule in the centre of the weapon brackets. This can be used to track targets and determine when to fire.
Weapons can be bound automatically to deploy the hardpoint when a trigger is fired, rather than manually deploying the hardpoint first.
It is good practice to retract hardpoints when in the vicinity of a starport, to prevent accidental fire zone infractions. All hardpoints must be retracted prior to entering supercruise.
Targeting $BINDING_input_either:#value=SELECTTARGET; allows the ship computer to track the position and status of an object. This is done by manually targeting once within range.

When an object is within your targeting reticule, you can lock into it manually. Alternatively, you can select a target from the Contacts tab on the External interface panel. This adds a marker to the target on your scanner display and provides some basic information about the target. Only a single object can be targeted at a time.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_basicequi: Provides a ship with the firepower needed to destroy opposing ships.
Forms a protective energy shield around the vessel, which continually regenerates while powered.
Hand-held weapons used in surface combat.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_defencear: Each ship model has a base armour hardness value which cannot be directly altered. The armour rating of a ship is the amount of protection provided against attack.

All weapons have a pierce rating, which dictates how effective they are against armour. If a weapon's pierce rating is above a targeted ship's armour rating, all of its damage will be dealt to the ship. If not, the armour rating will be subtracted from the pierce rating to determine the amount of damage to the ship.

Explosive weapons such as missiles, torpedoes and mines are effective armour-piercing weapons. These deal increased damage to internal modules and distribute damage over a large area of a target's hull. Railguns are also a highly effective armour-piercing weapon with a focused impact point, allowing individual modules to be targeted and destroyed.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_defencesh: A ship can have one Shield Generator installed. The strength of a shield is related to the generator's class and strength. When powered, a shield generator maintains a protective field around the ship. Each time a shield is struck, whether through weapons fire or collisions, the field's bond is weakened. Shields regenerate over time. Power is drawn from the ship to maintain the shield's maximum strength. If enough successive hits are scored on a shield to reduce its integrity to zero, the shield temporarily collapses. A broken shield causes the shield generator to reset.

Shields are represented in the cockpit HUD as blue circles around a ship schematic. When a shield collapses, the rings turn red and display a 'Recharging' status. The ring will gradually fill until the shield can be reformed.
Shields are more effective against kinetic attacks than thermal attacks.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_interdict: Interdiction is the act of locking onto another ship's supercruise vector and forcing them to disengage the frame shift drive. This is an illegal but valuable technique through which pirates can ambush ships. Traders and miners are common targets, with these pilots often carrying plenty of cargo to plunder.

The Frame Shift Interdictor is required to perform this action. The module must be assigned to a fire group and triggered when behind and in range of a target. When interdiction begins the HUD gains two new elements, an escape vector and alignment progress bars.

To win the interdiction you must keep the escape vector aligned with the centre of the HUD, the longer the escape vector stays in this position the more the blue progress bar grows. If the red bar hits maximum the target ship will escape. If the blue progress bar hits maximum your ship and the target ship will be dragged out of supercruise. The target ship will have to wait for their frame shift drive to reboot before they can escape back into supercruise.
Pirates themselves are at risk of interdiction, however. As they accrue bounties for their crimes, a pirate becomes an attractive target for system authorities and bounty hunters.

When this occurs filling the blue bar will allow you to escape being interdicted. Should the red bar fill first you will be pulled out of supercruise instead. You can submit to the interdiction by reducing your throttle to zero. Doing this will drastically decrease the amount of time you must wait for your FSD to reboot.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_introduct: Some independent fighters choose to participate in mercenary work, offering their services to factions in conflict for financial reward. Conflict zones appear in systems where war has broken out, allowing mercenaries to choose a faction to side with and enter the fray with weapons blazing.

When a Commander participates in the destruction of a target pledged to the opposing faction, they are rewarded with a combat bond. These bonds can be handed in at local starports and surface facilities in exchange for credits.

Commanders will need to rely heavily on their combat skills if they intend to make a career out of mercenary work. Mercenaries looking for work from mission providers or through the mission board should pay attention to the following mission types: • Assassination/Takedown, which offers a specific target which must be taken out within a set time frame. • Sabotage, requesting the destruction of a specific generator type or disruption of production at a planetary settlement. Locations are typically well defended. • Shutdown, which involves bringing a planetary settlement offline. • Massacre/Raid, targeting faction members at planetary surface locations. • Generator Sabotage, requesting the destruction of a specific generator type at a planetary settlement. Locations are typically well defended. • Onslaught, relevant to space conflict zones which can be found at starports in the system where war or civil war is occurring. Each faction involved in the conflict may provide missions to eliminate opposing forces. • Protect, where a settlement needs assistance in defending an important item against a hostile raid. These missions are time sensitive and involve heavy combat.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_mercact_r: Conflict zones in space are fleet battles that occur within a system where minor factions are engaged in war or civil war. This provides mercenary pilots with the opportunity to undertake missions for either side, earning credits and reputation.
Conflict zones are divided into three categories of intensity: Low, Medium and High. This indicates the number of ships fighting within a particular zone.
To locate a conflict zone, check the galaxy map for any system with the state of War or Civil War. To do this:

• Open the Galaxy Map from the External interface panel • Select the Map Mode tab • Choose the States overlay from the provided options • Filter for War and Civil War from the list of states • Systems with these states will now be highlighted on the map

Missions relevant to conflict zones can be found on the mission boards at starports in the system where the war is occurring. Each faction involved in the conflict may provide missions to eliminate opposing forces.

When entering a conflict zone, pilots will be presented with a message in the notification tab of the comms panel. This will offer the option to join a side in the conflict. Choosing a side determines which ships will appear as allies and which will appear as enemies.
Conflict zones have a status, denoting which side is currently winning the battle. Should one side triumph, the defeated side will flee the zone.

For each enemy ship a pilot directly destroys - or helps to destroy - during a conflict, a combat bond will be issued. These can be redeemed for credits at any station in the system where the issuing faction has a presence. Reputation with a faction will also rise upon delivery of combat bonds.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_powerman_: Pilots are able to configure the amount of energy distributed to each of the ship's three main power systems. This affects the functionality of each module.

• SYS (System power): Contributes to incoming damage reduction, shield strength and shield recharge rate. Also powers utility mount function. • ENG (Engine power): Contributes to the speed of a ship and the recharge rate of a ship's boost function. • WEP (Weapon power): Contributes to the weapon coolant system. This allows longer firing periods before thermal overload occurs.

The power assigned to each of these systems can be seen in the interface of the ship's cockpit, with pips displaying how much power is being supplied to each system. 6 full pips can be distributed across the three systems at any one time, with each individual system holding 4 pips maximum. In addition, the RST option will reset the power distribution settings, equalising power across the ship's systems.

The Power Distributor is responsible for distributing the energy generated by your ship. Higher classes and ratings increase the system's power capacitor and rate of recharge.
Removing all power from any ship's system will not cause the associated modules to go offline. However, it will cause an effect:

• Diverting power from SYS will prevent shields from recharging once the capacitor is depleted.
• Diverting power from ENG will reduce the maximum speed and manoeuvrability of a ship, and will prevent the boost function from recharging.
• Diverting power from WEP will increase the likelihood of overheating, reducing their firing rate.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_precis: How to be a combat pilot for hire in a dangerous galaxy.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_surfaceco: Combatants engage on a planet’s surface using hand-held weaponry, protected by the shielding and armour of their suits.

Removed from the many ship functions available to combat pilots, surface combatants must instead rely on their mobility and accuracy. Personal weapons are not gimballed, targets are not autonomously tracked and there are no fire groups to set.  Instead, the use of cover, suit radar awareness and health management become key skills in surviving a firefight.

Equipment A variety of weapons, suits and consumable extras are available. Combat-focused Commanders should consider the Manticore Dominator suit for its extra weapon options and survivability. See the Suit Equipment guide for more information.

Surface Recon Vehicles, or SRVs, are also useful vehicles for surface combat. They offer additional protection and manoeuvrability along with a mounted turret, but can be vulnerable to explosive damage and higher grades of weapons.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_surfacecz:
<font size='20' color='#f8f8f8'>RESUPPLY</font>
Various caches, crates and boxes will allow you to resupply ammo, energy and health. Recharge sockets are also present to restore suit energy via the energylink tool.

<font size='20' color='#f8f8f8'>BETWEEN ROUNDS</font>
When defeated, you will have the option to rejoin the battle from a dropship, switch your current loadout, or retreat from the conflict zone. A deployment counter indicates the time until your return to the fight.

<font size='20' color='#f8f8f8'>CONFLICT END</font>
Once a battle is concluded, the conflict zone statistics screen is available to view. If you arrived via a Frontline Solutions dropship you will be collected and returned to the starport you enlisted at. Otherwise you will be able to recall your ship.

Surface conflict zones are localised engagements at a strategic settlement. Coordinating stellar conflicts requires a huge amount of communication data, which is channelled through specific network routes. Alongside a faction’s own security forces, mercenaries are hired to secure this data using force.
HOW TO JOIN Follow the steps outlined on the Conflict Zones - Space page to identify a system in conflict. There are two options to join a surface conflict zone:

Frontline Solutions Found at the starport concourse, this service makes joining a conflict zone simple. You can select a conflict to join and a faction to fight for before boarding a shuttle to carry you straight to the fight. See the Frontline Solutions page of the Concourse guide for more information.

Manual Entry Arriving at a settlement with an active conflict will allow you to access the Conflict Zone Stats screen $BINDING_input_either:#value=HumanoidConflictContextualUIButton;. From you can select a faction to fight for. Alternatively simply eliminating a combatant will automatically sign you up with the opposite faction.

<font size='20' color='#f8f8f8'>OBJECTIVES</font>
Each surface conflict zone is assigned a set amount of resources by the two opposing factions. This represents the level of reinforcements a faction is willing to commit to claim the settlement’s comms data. When one faction forces the other to 0 reinforcements it declares victory.

CONTROL POINTS As data is acquired through the capture of control points, the reinforcements a faction is willing to pledge in pursuit of the remaining data falls. When a capture point activates it will appear on your suit’s Insight display.

• A green control point is being claimed by your faction 
• A red control point is bring claimed by the enemy
• A yellow point is being actively contested by both factions

Capturing a control point requires at least one member of a team to remain in the control point’s capture area while it is clear of enemies.  100 points are removed from the enemy action’s reinforcement level once a control point is captured.

Eliminating an enemy is worth a single reinforcement point.
codex_pilotshandbook_mercenary_weapontyp: There are four weapon types: Thermal, Kinetic, Thermal-Kinetic and Explosive. These types have various strengths and weaknesses, with some more suited to certain situations than others.

Thermal Weapons Thermal weapons require no ammunition, but they do use a capacitor charge provided by the ship's power plant. If this charge is spent, it must be recharged to allow the weapon to continue firing. These weapons are the most effective means of stripping away shields but are less successful against hulls. A common tactic is to deploy thermal weapons to remove a target's shield prior to using kinetic weapons against its hull. Examples of thermal weapons include beam lasers, pulse lasers and burst lasers. A mining laser is also capable of delivering damage to a ship but is not designed for combat

Kinetic Weapons Kinetic weapons require ammunition to function, but consume less energy and produce less heat than thermal weapons. They are the most efficient means of damaging a target ship's hull but are less effective against shields. Examples of kinetic weapons include multi-cannons and fragment cannons. Ammunition can be replenished at stations or synthesised.

Thermal-Kinetic Weapons Thermal-kinetic weapons are capable of dealing very high damage to both a target's shield and hull. They require both ammunition and energy and produce a lot of heat. Examples of thermal-kinetic weapons include railguns and plasma accelerators. Ammunition can be replenished at stations or synthesised.

Explosive Weapons Explosive weapons require ammunition and produce a large amount of heat when fired. However, they consume little energy and are capable of dealing high damage to a target's hull. Examples of explosive weapons include missile racks, torpedo pylons and mine launchers. Missiles come in two types:

• Dumbfire, which shoot directly forward immediately after firing and impact with full damage. • Seeker, which will lock onto a target and follow their trajectory, but require several seconds to establish a lock and impact with slightly less damage.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_abrasionblast: <font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>EXAMPLE OF A SURFACE DEPOSIT</font>
Abrasion blasters are used to extricate surface deposits. Simply aim them at an asteroid surface deposit and fire. A successful hit will dislodge resources for collection.
Analysis mode must be activated $BINDING_input_either:#value=PlayerHUDModeToggle; to use the Abrasion Blaster.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_basicmining_d: Using your ship's mining laser or a mining rig, it is possible to extract resource deposits from the surface of an asteroid or from a planetary body.
When mining from an asteroid, these resources can then be collected using the cargo scoop. Resources are deposited into a refinery bin, forming the resource into a unit of cargo when full.
This unit of cargo is then transferred automatically into your cargo hold.
On many worlds, mineral wealth lies buried beneath the surface and out of reach of a ship's mining laser. Extracting it requires an SRV capable of deploying a laser mining rig.
See the Surface Mining section for further information.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_deepcore_desc: Fires charges into asteroid fissures. The subsequent detonation reveals deep core deposits.

Deep core mining involves using seismic charges on asteroid fissures. The power of the charge – low, medium or high – is determined by how long you hold the trigger. As you fire charges into the fissures, you should see the detonation yield indicator in the top-right of your HUD approach the blue area. Fissures can be low, medium or high strength, denoting their resistance to charges.
High charge in low-strength fissure = maximum effectiveness, large increase to detonation yield.
Low charge in high-strength fissure = minimum effectiveness, slight increase to detonation yield.

Once a charge has been placed, a chart appears in the top-right corner of the HUD, at which point you have 120 seconds to finish planting charges. The ship's computer calculates the optimal yield range for the task at hand and displays it as a blue bar in the chart. If the level is below this range when you detonate your charges, the asteroid will remain intact. On the other hand, if the level is above the blue bar, many of the valuable resources within will be destroyed.

If adjustments need to be made, charges can be disabled after they have been fired. Note that any charges you do not disable will automatically detonate at the end of the countdown. Once the charges detonate, exposed resources can be harvested using standard mining techniques.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_essentialequi: Emits a pulse from your SRV that detects subsurface deposits at range and returns their location to the sensors. Deposits already exhausted will not register.
Carves out resources (and occasionally Engineer materials) from the surface of an asteroid.

Firing the mining laser at an asteroid will carve resource deposits from the surface of the asteroid. Analysis mode must be activated $BINDING_input_either:#value=PlayerHUDModeToggle; to use the mining laser.
Refines resources into sellable cargo. Resources are stored in bins, the number of which is determined by the class of your module.

The refinery is displayed in the right-side panel. This shows the resources in your refinery, which bins they're in, and how much of each type of resource you have. If you have insufficient bin space when attempting to gather resources, you can choose to either empty a bin to make space, or abandon the resource chunk.
Drills into the surface and extracts mineral deposits, which it stores until recovered.

Deployed from an SRV while within the bounds of a scanned deposit. The rig automatically deploys once the SRV has driven clear and begins work automatically. Efficiency may be improved on foot with an energy link.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_introduction_: Mining allows pilots to gather resources from asteroid belts and planetary rings using lasers, blasters and explosives. These resources are then refined into units of cargo. While considered a reasonably safe career path, experienced miners keep an eye on their radar for pirates looking to claim hard-earned cargo for themselves.

Commanders can use refined cargo for trade on the Commodities Market, to fulfil a mission requirement, or to contribute to a Community Goal. Pilots looking for work via the mission board should pay attention to the following mission types: • Mining, in which materials must be extracted from asteroids and then delivered to a set destination.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_optequiplimp_: COLLECTOR LIMPET CONTROLLER Optional Internal Module (various)
Deploys limpets to gather up any loose resources or material and return them to your ship. Collector limpets are used to pick up any resources in your vicinity. Limpets have two modes:

Targeted: The limpet collects the item you have targeted $BINDING_input_either:#value=SELECTTARGET; and returns it to your ship. Untargeted: The limpet takes up position outside your ship and automatically gathers any resources in the area.

You can program limpets to ignore unwanted resources via the Contacts tab in the left-side panel. If there are no valid targets within range, collector limpets will attempt to follow their parent ship for a short period before eventually expiring. If you have no limpets available, you can collect resources manually using your ship's cargo scoop.
PROSPECTOR LIMPET CONTROLLER Optional Internal Module (various)

Controls limpets that can determine the composition of an asteroid.

Select an asteroid and fire a prospector limpet at it. When the limpet is attached it will display all resources and fissures on the asteroid.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_optequipscan_: Launches probes, while in supercruise, that scan planetary belts and highlight hotspots.

While in supercruise, bring your ship within range of the mining location and throttle down. Then use the Detailed Surface Scanner to fire a probe at the planetary ring. Any mining hotspots will be displayed both in the ring and in your Navigation panel. Hotspots mean higher-yield asteroids and a greater number of asteroids with deep core deposits. Note that asteroid belts cannot be probed in this way and must be investigated manually.
Emits a spherical pulse of energy that highlights asteroids containing resource deposits.
Analysis Mode must also be activated $BINDING_input_either:#value=PlayerHUDModeToggle; to use the Pulse Wave Analyser. This highlights potential deposits within all asteroids in your immediate area.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_precis: A guide to mining throughout the galaxy.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_scoopcargo_de: The cargo scoop must be deployed $BINDING_input_either:#value=TOGGLECARGOSCOOP; before items can be collected. This can also be done via the ship's Functions menu. Targeting the desired cargo $BINDING_input_either:#value=SELECTTARGET; will initiate the scoop guidance interface once within range.

A slow approach towards the targeted cargo is recommended. The interface tracks the cargo's position in relation to your scoop, allowing the pilot to align cargo with the guidance reticule. When the cargo is safely onboard, the scoop automatically loads it into your cargo racks.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_subsurface_de: Bore into an asteroid to explosively extract sub-surface deposits.
Sub-surface missiles are fired at targeted sub-surface deposits. Once embedded, they transmit data to the lower left-hand side of your HUD.
The top part shows the rock density, determining the speed of the sub-surface drill.

The bottom part shows the progress of the drill, and will move faster or slower depending on the speed of the drilling indicated above. The blue area shows a deposit resource, while the width of the blue area indicates the quality of the resource.
Releasing the trigger and detonating the missile while the bar is in the blue will dislodge any resources.
Analysis mode must be activated to use the Sub-Surface Displacement Missile Launcher.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_surfacemining: Surface mining extracts minerals from beneath the crust of a planetary body. It requires an SRV capable of deploying and recovering a laser mining rig.

Rigs operate at a baseline efficiency of one hundred per cent. Extreme temperatures will reduce this. Disembarking and applying an energy link to a rig will raise its efficiency, however, overcharging will lower efficiency below baseline until the excess energy has bled off automatically. The rig's current efficiency is displayed on your HUD and on the rig itself.
A rig will signal when it is full or when it has exhausted the deposit. Each is marked on your sensors and may be left in place and recovered later.
Recovery is initiated from the Contacts tab of the left-hand panel. Bring the SRV to within a hundred metres and the rig will automatically prepare for collection.
Recovered minerals are transferred to the SRV's onboard refinery and processed into cargo. Be aware that if the refinery has no capacity, any surplus will be lost.
Rigs are not armoured, and a destroyed one is lost along with its contents. A rig will also be lost if the SRV strays too far from it, or if the SRV itself is destroyed or returns to its mothership.
Locate a Planetary Mining Location from orbit by mapping the planetary body with a Detailed Surface Scanner, then land within it and deploy your SRV.
A surface mining SRV carries a built-in scanner. Activating it emits a pulse that registers any Planetary Mining Deposit within several kilometres and returns their bearing to your sensors.
Once a deposit is within range it can be targeted and scanned to reveal its composition.
Deposits vary considerably in size, from a few metres across to 300 metres maximum.

Deploy a mining rig from your SRV while within range of the deposit. The rig is released beneath the SRV will unpack and deploy automatically once you have driven clear of it. It begins drilling as soon as it is fully deployed, storing the extracted deposits internally.
Several rigs can be deployed at once.
codex_pilotshandbook_miner_wheretomine_d: Mining is conducted in asteroid belt clusters or planetary rings. To identify a suitable mining location, open the System Map and select a ringed planet or asteroid belt.
Once a body has been mapped, its Mineral Fields can be selected from the navigation panel or viewed in Subsurface Resources analysis mode. Selecting a field displays the minerals present within it.

Composition varies with the nature of the planetary body. Volcanism, atmosphere and the material content of the crust all determine what can be extracted, and nearby stellar bodies can also affect a world's geology.
The following information is displayed in the System Map on the Details screen when selected:

• Rocky: Ores, industrial minerals and gemstones. • Icy: Water, gasses and low-temperature crystalline compounds. • Rocky Ice: Water and ices alongside common metals. • Metal rich: Precious and heavy metals in abundance. • High Metal Content: Common and industrial metals.

Mineral Fields are graded by reserve level in the same manner as asteroid belts and planetary rings, and this is displayed in the System Map and in planetary information. A field that has been fully worked will register as depleted.
Surface mining is conducted on the surfaces of planetary bodies. Deposits are not evenly distributed.

To locate them, target a body and conduct a Detailed Surface Scan. Mapping the surface reveals any Planetary Mining Location present where mineral extraction is viable. Most planetary bodies hold more than one.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_advequip_des: FRAME SHIFT DRIVE INTERDICTOR Optional Internal
Attempts to pull target ships out of supercruise, rendering them vulnerable to the pirate's demands. The effective interdiction range is determined by the module's class and rating.
HATCH BREAKER LIMPET CONTROLLER Optional Internal

Fires limpets which attach themselves to a target's cargo hatch, forcing it open and liberating a portion of the cargo inside. The effective range of limpets is determined by the controller's class and rating.
Deploys limpets to gather up any available cargo canisters and return them to your ship.
Analyses a ship's cargo hold, helping to determine suitable candidates for piracy.

Once added to a fire group the manifest scanner can be fired at a targeted ship. Once the scan is complete you can inspect the contents of the target's cargo hold in the Target tab of the External interface panel, found to the left of the cockpit chair.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_basicequip_d: Provides a ship with the firepower needed to threaten or subdue a target, and to damage a target's cargo hold.
Holds cargo canisters obtained from targets, allowing for their transport to a black market for sale.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_basicpiracy_: Acts of piracy can occur anywhere in the galaxy. As ships generally carry cargo reflective of the station economies they visit, it can be lucrative for pirates to prowl the shipping lanes between wealthy starports and outposts which import expensive goods. High value targets can often be found in systems experiencing the following states: • Investment • Boom • Expansion • Civil War • Election • Civil Liberty • Expansion

Pirates typically select and outfit ships with strong offensive and defensive capabilities, while also seeking the agility to maintain the pursuit of their targets. They must also consider the cargo space required to carry their ill-gotten gains.

System security should be considered when choosing a suitable location. The current security level determines how swiftly system authorities will respond to criminal acts taking place in their space. Piracy is therefore rife in anarchy systems, where no such authorities exist and bounties will not be issued against criminal acts.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_interdiction: Interdiction is the act of locking onto another ship's supercruise vector and forcing them to disengage the frame shift drive. This is an illegal but valuable technique through which pirates can ambush ships. Traders and miners are common targets, with these pilots often carrying plenty of cargo to plunder.

The Frame Shift Interdictor is required to perform this action. The module must be assigned to a fire group and triggered when behind and in range of a target. When interdiction begins the HUD gains two new elements, an escape vector and alignment progress bars.

To win the interdiction you must keep the escape vector aligned with the centre of the HUD, the longer the escape vector stays in this position the more the blue progress bar grows. If the red bar hits maximum the target ship will escape. If the blue progress bar hits maximum your ship and the target ship will be dragged out of supercruise. The target ship will have to wait for their frame shift drive to reboot before they can escape back into supercruise.
Pirates themselves are at risk of interdiction, however. As they accrue bounties for their crimes, a pirate becomes an attractive target for system authorities and bounty hunters.

When this occurs filling the blue bar will allow you to escape being interdicted. Should the red bar fill first you will be pulled out of supercruise instead. You can submit to the interdiction by reducing your throttle to zero. Doing this will drastically decrease the amount of time you must wait for your FSD to reboot.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_intro_descri: Piracy is the theft of cargo from other ships through threats, force or, when required, a combination of the two. Cargo is obtained from the target's hold, either willingly provided by the pilot or following a cargo hatch breach. It is an illegal yet potentially lucrative career which can be performed anywhere in the galaxy where other ships are present. Piracy is a challenging career path and requires great skill and technique.

Commanders can sell the stolen cargo at a black market, found at any station where criminals offer this service. Pilots looking for criminal activities may find the following mission types interesting: • Data Theft, where data must be obtained from a hostile location by scanning a data point. • Theft, in which cargo must be taken from a target or group, usually by force.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_obtaincargo_: Once a target's cargo has been identified via the Manifest Scanner and the ship subsequently engaged, a pirate generally has two approaches: force a ship to jettison cargo, or convince their target to do so for them.
Cargo canisters can be gathered with collector limpets or via the cargo scoop. Collector limpets are much more efficient but do take up precious space in a ship's loadout and hold.

Destroying a ship will also result in the loss of any cargo they carry. Therefore, weapons should be utilised with restraint to prevent the loss of a profitable haul. Any non-Anarchy system will also issue a bounty for blowing another ship apart without due cause.

Damaging a ship's cargo hatch sufficiently will result in cargo being ejected from the hold. It is advisable to cease fire at this point, as further damage to a hatch which is currently ejecting cargo will not increase the yield. When cargo canisters have stopped appearing, additional damage to the hatch will trigger a fresh batch of jettisoned cargo.

Hatch breaker limpets are used to crack open a target's cargo hatch, releasing a portion of the cargo inside. Hatch breakers have a speed of 300m/s and can pass through shields; they can only be stopped with point defences or electronic countermeasures.

Following a successful scan of the target ship, a pirate selects the Cargo Hatch sub-target. The limpet is then deployed, where it will attempt to latch itself onto a target's cargo hatch. If successful, the limpet will pry the hatch open, releasing cargo for collection.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_piratecmdrs_: When pirating other Commanders, demonstrating superior firepower or speed can intimidate the target commander and cause them to voluntarily surrender cargo in an effort to appease the pirate. The benefit of this approach is acquiring cargo without needing to subdue a target through force, while the victim minimises any risk of destruction and/or the loss of their entire payload.
A moving ship will eject cargo over a much wider area, so an experienced pirate will try to force a target ship to hold position before extorting cargo from them.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_precis: A guide to taking other people's things and avoiding the law.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_scoopcargo_d: The cargo scoop must be deployed $BINDING_input_either:#value=TOGGLECARGOSCOOP; before items can be collected. This can also be done via the ship's Functions menu. Targeting the desired cargo $BINDING_input_either:#value=SELECTTARGET; will initiate the scoop guidance interface once within range.

Using the scooping guidance interface to measure your position in relaction to the cargo, you should slowly move towards the target. When the cargo is safely onboard, the scoop automatically loads it into your cargo racks.
codex_pilotshandbook_pirate_sellingcargo: Cargo robbed from other pilots must be sold on the black market. Some starports will host a contact providing access to this marketplace, where stolen or prohibited goods can be sold.
The price of items on the black market can vary, depending on the goods being traded and the demands of the system.
Stations which feature a black market can be found in the galaxy map via the following method:

• Open the Galaxy Map from the External interface panel • Select the Map Mode tab • Choose the Services overlay from the provided options • Select Black Market from the list of services • Systems with black markets will now be highlighted on the map

Carrying stolen goods is risky. System authorities will often scan the cargo of ships to check if they are carrying stolen/prohibited goods. If discovered, a pilot carrying such goods will be issued with a fine or bounty.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_activitie:
Activities are the means by which Power Agents can influence systems involved in Powerplay and apply control score changes to them.
Each activity involved in Powerplay can be performed to either Acquire, Reinforce or Undermine. Powers will have preferred activities for each of these actions, see Power Ethos, but an agent can undertake any activity to perform an action they just won't receive the bonus if it is not one of their Powers Ethos activities.
Listed below are all the Powerplay activities grouped by the actions they can be performed for.
Sell for Large Profits - Sell commodities in systems that your Power can Acquire for a profit of 40% or higher.

Sell Mined Resources - Sell mined commodities in systems that your Power can Acquire. These goods must have been mined, not purchased from a market, in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power that is in control range of the Acquirable system then sold in the Acquirable system.
Sell Rare Goods - Sell Rare Goods commodities in systems that your Power can Acquire. These commodities cannot come from the same system they are being sold to.

Transfer Power Classified Data - Download data from data ports at settlements your Power can acquire and return them to a Power contact in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power that is in control range of the Acquirable system.

Transfer Power Association and Political Data - Download data from data ports at settlements your Power can acquire and return them to a Power contact in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power that is in control range of the Acquirable system.

Transfer Power Research and Industrial Data - Download data from data ports at settlements your Power can acquire and return them to a Power contact in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power that is in control range of the Acquirable system.

Transport Power Commodities - Requisition your Powers Acquisition commodity from a Power contact at a port in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power that is in control range of the system you want to Acquire and deliver it to a Power contact in that system.

Upload Powerplay-Specific Malware - Requisition Power Injection Malware data from a Power contact at a port in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power and upload it to data ports at settlements in a system your Power can Acquire.
Acquisition (Conflict): The following activities can be performed in a system that your power can Acquire and where your Power is in conflict with at least one other Power.
Complete Aid and Humanitarian Missions - Complete altruism, aid and humanitarian missions in systems that your Power can Acquire.
ACQUISITION
Flood Markets with Low Value Goods - Sell commodities worth less than 500 credits at markets in systems that your Power can Acquire.

Scan Ships and Wakes - Scan ships, high energy wakes and low energy wakes scans in systems that your Power can Acquire. Ships and low energy wakes can be scanned using the default scanning function on all ships. A Frame Shift Wake Scanner is required to scan high energy wakes.
REINFORCEMENT
Bounty Hunting - Collect bounty vouchers, see bounty hunting in the pilot’s handbook. You do not need to hand in the vouchers.

Collect Escape Pods - Collect escape pods from the system your Power controls that you want to Reinforce and deliver them to a Power contact in the same system. Refer to the Salvage and Rescue article in the Pilot's Handbook for more information on collecting cargo.

Hand in Biological Research Samples - Collect Biological Samples and deliver them to a Vista Genomics outlet in systems your Power controls.

Hand in Cartography Data - Sell exploration data at any system your Power controls via a port's Universal Cartographics service. Refer to the Exploration article in the Pilot's Handbook for more information on scanning celestial bodies and selling exploration data.

Hand in Salvage - Collect salvage from the system your Power controls that you want to Reinforce and deliver them to a Power contact in the same system. Refer to the Salvage and Rescue article in the Pilot's Handbook for more information on collecting cargo.
Holoscreen Hacking - Hack already hacked holographic adverts at ports in systems that your Power controls to reset them. A recon limpet controller is required to hack holoscreens.
Bounty Hunting - Collect bounty vouchers in systems that your Power can Acquire, see bounty hunting in the pilot’s handbook. You do not need to hand in the vouchers.
Power Kills - Kill vessels and personnel aligned with Powers you are not pledged to in systems your Power controls.
Reboot Mission Completion - Complete reboot missions in systems that your Power controls.

Scan Ships and Wakes - Scan ships, high energy wakes and low energy wakes scans in any system controlled by your Power that you want to Reinforce. Ships and low energy wakes can be scanned using the default scanning function on all ships. A Frame Shift Wake Scanner is required to scan high energy wakes.
Sell for Large Profits - Sell commodities in systems that your Power controls for a profit of 40% or higher.
Sell Mined Resources - Sell mined commodities in systems that your Power controls. These goods must have been mined, not purchased from a market, in the same system you want to Reinforce.
Sell Rare Goods - Sell Rare Goods commodities in systems that your Power controls. These commodities cannot come from the same system they are being sold to.
Transfer Power Classified Data - Download data from data ports at settlements in your Power's controlled systems and return them to the Power Contact in the same system.
Transfer Power Association and Political Data - Download data from data ports at settlements in your Power's controlled systems and return them to the Power Contact in the same system.

Transport Power Commodities - Requisition your Powers Reinforcement commodity from a Power contact in a Stronghold system controlled by your Power and deliver it to a Power contact in the system you want to Reinforce. Powerplay commodities cannot be handed into the same system they are collected from.
UNDERMINING

Collect Escape Pods - Collect escape pods from the Acquisition system and deliver them to a Power contact in a Fortified or Stronghold system controlled by your Power within control range of the Acquisition system. Refer to the Salvage and Rescue article in the Pilot's Handbook for more information on collecting cargo.

Collect Escape Pods - Collect Occupied Escape Pods and Damaged Escape Pods in systems controlled by a Power that you are not pledged to. The pods will count towards your total once scooped into your vessel's cargo hold. Refer to the Salvage and Rescue article in the Pilot's Handbook for more information on collecting cargo.
Commit Crimes - Commit Crimes in systems controlled by Powers that you are not pledged to.

Holoscreen Hacking - Hack holographic adverts at ports in systems controlled by Powers that you are not pledged to. A recon limpet controller is required to hack holoscreens.
Power Kills - Kill vessels and personnel aligned with Powers you are not pledged to in systems controlled by Powers that you are not pledged to.

Scan Datalinks - Scan datalinks at Megaships in systems controlled by Powers that you are not pledged to.
