<font size='40'>ACTIVITIES</font>
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_assignmen: Tasks that your Power has asked you to complete to aid in their efforts are called assignments. Completed assignments will reward you with merits, which are used to measure your effort and track your loyalty progress with your chosen Power. Merits are also earned by engaging in Powerplay activities that benefit your Power.

Assignments listed in this section will offer your current progress on each, information about how and where to complete a task and the offered reward. This information can also be found in the Transactions tab of the External interface panel.
Once pledged to a Power, you must complete an initial set of assignments before you are considered a full member.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_control_d: Powers aim to control as many systems as possible. Within each system, a Power can solidify their influence through three levels of control: Exploited, Fortified and Stronghold.

To fully control systems, Powers perform reinforcement activities in systems they have Exploited until it progresses to the Fortified state and eventually the Stronghold state. This allows a Power to expand into neighbouring systems but also protects it – Exploited systems that are outside the control range of a friendly Fortified or Stronghold system will become uncontrolled at the end of the active weekly cycle. Reinforcement activities also counter undermining efforts by other Powers in the system seeking to gain control.

Strongholds are candidates for housing a stronghold carrier fleet, which grant docking permission to supporters of the controlling Power only. These offer access to improved outfitting and shipyard inventories when compared to most ports. At the end of each weekly cycle a stronghold system with the highest control score will be assigned a carrier fleet, providing that this would not overlap with the control range of another carrier owned by that Power.

When completing activities to undermine another Power’s control, a defensive modifier is used to determine how effective undermining actions are in the local system. This is calculated based on how developed the system is and how far it is from your Power’s nearest fortified or stronghold system. A system can only change by one Control state per weekly cycle.

Systems that lack or lose a controlled state become Uncontrolled, which are prime expansion candidates for all nearby Powers. If the control radius of a fortified or stronghold system contains an uncontrolled system, then it is a viable target for acquisition via standard powerplay activities. Multiple Powers can compete simultaneously to acquire a system; if two or more Powers reach the conflict threshold then conflict zones will spawn between all eligible Powers. Each Power will also utilize conflict activities based on its ethos, offering supporters new ways to increase its score in the system. Various Powerplay activities will award different score values based on how difficult they are to complete.

To successfully gain control of a system, a Power must reach a minimum target threshold and be ahead of all other Power’s scores at the end of the weekly cycle. If the minimum threshold is not reached, then all activity scores rollover to the following week’s cycle. This continues until a Power establishes control.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_ethos_des: A Power’s Ethos is heavily influenced by that Power’s leader. Their morals, ideals and history inform the doctrine of the Power and determine how their followers tend to operate in Powerplay.

While a Power’s agents can advance their goals by performing any Powerplay activity relevant to the system they are in, by adhering to their Ethos they will typically have a greater impact on those systems - and earn more merits for doing so.

These ethos activities are highlighted in the Powerplay Information panel, found in the Galaxy map. When a system is selected while using the Powerplay map mode, the Powerplay Information panel will be available in the list of target information tabs on the right side of the screen.

When Undermining a system Agents will have access to Ethos bonuses for two additional activities based on the Power that is being Undermined. These activities will be listed in the Powerplay Information panel on the galaxy map when an appropriate system is selected.

When attempting to Acquire a system in the Acquisition Contested state Agents will have access to Ethos bonuses for two additional activities based on their Power. These activities will be listed in the Powerplay Information panel on the galaxy map when an appropriate system is selected.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_introduct: Powerplay represents the continuous struggle for influence and prestige in populated star systems. Powers seek to establish control over systems, undermine the efforts of rival Powers eager to do the same, and reinforce controlled areas to maintain superiority.

Powers offer rewards to those pledged to them, with loyal supporters who contribute to a Power’s success earning more potent and numerous rewards. Loyalty is determined by the number of merits a supporter receives for completing Powerplay activities.

Expanding the territory of a Power increases the systems in which agents of that Power can benefit from these rewards. Strengthening a Power's level of control over a system also expands the range within which rival territory or uncontrolled systems can be targeted for undermining or acquisition.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_leaderboa: Leaderboards are unlocked by achieving the first loyalty rank after completing your Power’s introductory assignments.

Each week, a Power will keep track of all merits earned through Powerplay activities, and rank supporters of the Power accordingly. The leaderboard is the visual for this competition between agents of a Power, and is intended to celebrate those who earn the most merits in a weekly cycle.

The final position on the leaderboard impacts the size of the reward granted at the end of the weekly cycle. Those dedicated agents who make it into the top 10 will be proudly displayed for the following week’s cycle.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_loyalty_d: The Loyalty screen displays your current rank with your chosen Power. This represents the recognition by your Power for all efforts you have made to advance its standing in the galaxy.
As you gain merits your loyalty rank will increase. After the first five ranks, the merit requirement to advance a rank becomes consistent.

Each time you gain a new rank, your Power will grant a reward to honour your dedication to its cause. These rewards include perks that provide various bonuses in certain systems, access to unique modules, and care packages containing useful materials and credits.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_powerinfo: The Power Information screen provides an overview of your chosen Power. Here you can remind yourself of the Power’s ethos and review the potential rewards earned by achieving more ranks.
You also have the option to leave your current chosen Power from this screen. Leaving a Power removes all earned perks and unique module access, while your current merits and rank will reset to zero.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_powerplay:
The Power Overview screen is a portal to various information displays related to Powerplay. Here you’ll be able to:

- Check the current Power standings
- Evaluate a fill list of all systems eligible for Powerplay actions
- Review your active weekly Powerplay assignments
- Explore your available loyalty ranks and rewards
- View the currently weekly leaderboard for all agents of your chosen Power
- Review information about your chosen Power and its ethos
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_powers_de: At the height of humanities history in the 34th century, the political landscape was dominated by three Superpowers: The Federation led by democratically elected Presidents, their long-time waring rivals, the Empire, dynastically maintained by hereditary monarchies, and the Alliance which emerged from a much larger coalition of independent systems united politically by a desire for stability.

Whilst these Superpowers were a dominating force, they were not themselves unified. Each Superpower was itself built from sub-factions known as Powers. Even though these Powers may have been ideologically aligned in some cases their charismatic leaders also had their own agendas. These tensions between Powers, and indeed Superpowers, led to an era of territorial conflict.
When a Power assumes control of a system, it triggers temporary changes to local laws, economy and security levels while expanding its territory and overall influence.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_precis: An introduction to engaging with Powerplay.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_standings: The Power Standings section of the Overview screen ranks all twelve Powers by the number of systems they currently control. The Power with the most controlled systems is considered the most influential Power in the core systems. Supporters of the leading Power should take great pride in this achievement.
codex_pilotshandbook_powerplay_warroom_d: The Territory panel will send you to the Galaxy Map screen. Here you can review all star systems either in a state of Powerplay control or eligible for expansion by using the Powerplay map mode tab on the left-hand options.

Search filters for individual Powers or control states can be applied to find a system to conduct Powerplay activities in. Toggle these to find a system suiting the kind of activity you want to do, and the target of those actions. The second tab allows for you to filter by activity type and an additional option exists to filter by activity level. This shows systems where Powerplay Agents are actively engaging in Powerplay Activities

Selecting a system, followed by the Powerplay Information tab on the right-side options, will display:

- The system's current control state
- Which Power controls the system (if any)
- The current Control Score and projected control status at the end of the current cycle
- A list of activities that can be performed in the system to benefit your Power
If the system is currently contested, then the progress of the two leading Powers will be displayed alongside the conflict and victory thresholds required by each.

With a system selected, you can also toggle the Strategic View at the bottom of the Powerplay Information tab. This will display the system's control radius, used to determine eligible target systems for expansion. Unoccupied systems within the radius of a Fortified and Stronghold systems can be acquired by your Power.
codex_pilotshandbook_salvage_rescue_equi: Comes equipped with the arc cutter tool, used to cut open locked containers and access panels.
Provides storage space for cargo canisters, allowing their safe transportation. The number of cargo units held in each rack is determined by the module's class.
Deploys limpets to gather up any nearby cargo canisters and return them to your ship.

Ejects heatsinks, rapidly reducing a ship's heat levels. A low-temperature ship is harder to track and scan. Particularly useful for those salvaging illegal cargo who wish to minimise their heat signature.
Allows the transport of passengers. These cabins are required for transporting evacuees from damaged stations.
codex_pilotshandbook_salvage_rescue_intr: A lot can happen in the depths of space. Whether following combat, accidents, emergencies or sabotage, debris can be left behind for the intrepid salvage expert to collect. Surface operations are not immune to such dangers, with crash sites and inactive settlements commonly stripped of anything valuable. Sometimes this loot is fair game and can be legally traded; other times discovered goods and cargo are considered illegal and will require less traditional markets to offload.

Occasionally, the need arises for a pilot to retrieve escape pods. Whether recovered freely in space, collected on planet surfaces or rescued from megaships in a state of emergency, they are considered legal salvage and can be transported to a Search and Rescue Agent at stations for a reward.

Commanders can sell salvaged goods on the commodities market or black market, depending on legality. Concourse bartenders are known to fence illegal goods as well. Alternatively, these goods can be used to complete missions. Pilots looking to help recover valuable data or cargo may find the following mission types interesting: • Data Recovery, where data must be obtained from a hostile location by scanning a data point. • Cargo Liberation, where stolen cargo needs to be reclaimed from a specific target. • Salvage, a category of mission where an item must be recovered from a surface location or settlement.
codex_pilotshandbook_salvage_rescue_plan: Surface salvage refers to the retrieval of items or data on a planetary surface. There are some differences between salvage missions, depending on where the contract was accepted:

• Concourse terminal mission boards and mission providers will occasionally offer Salvage category missions to retrieve small legal or illegal items.
• Starport and local service mission boards may direct you to a surface location to collect a large item, which necessitates the use of an SRV.

Transporting illegal goods will incur fines or bounties if discovered within your suit inventory. See the Trade and Smuggling guide for information on transporting illegal goods.
FINDING SALVAGE Aside from missions, the two primary sources of finding salvage are offline settlements and planetary signal sources.

A ship’s detailed surface scanner will display planetary signal sources once a body has been fully mapped, along with the threat level associated with them. If your ship does not have this module then hovering 2-3km above the surface of a planet will reveal any signal sources in your general vicinity.

Offline settlements will be listed on the system map once you have scanned a planet or purchased the system’s data. The arc cutter is required to access any locked containers found at a salvage site. This comes as standard with the Remlok Maverick suit. See the Suit Equipment guide for more information.

Points of Interest Points of interest may sit within the boundary of a facility where access is prohibited, and trespassing may incur a fine or bounty – or even the hostility of any patrolling skimmers. Trespass zones are marked in red on a vehicle's scanner display when active on a planetary surface.
Cargo which can be potentially discovered at points of interest, such as cargo canisters or occupied escape pods, are usually considered legal salvage.
codex_pilotshandbook_salvage_rescue_prec: How to find salvage, and rescue the lost throughout a dangerous galaxy.
codex_pilotshandbook_salvage_rescue_proc: Commanders are often called upon to provide assistance in emergencies, or to recover pilots stranded throughout the galaxy. A variety of legal salvage can be picked up in rescue operations; escape pods, flight recorders and personal effects are all in need of recovery for a reward.
Occupied escape pods often require rescue from megaships that are in a state of emergency. These can be transported to a Search and Rescue Agent at stations in exchange for rewards.
Finding Rescue work A variety of signal sources can indicate escape pods are present.

• Degraded Emissions (USS) contain a variety of debris which can include jettisoned escape pods. • Points of interest are sometimes assigned to crashed spacecraft, with occupied escape pods present on occasion.

Damaged Megaships Megaships which have been damaged or are in a state of emergency will often eject escape pods. These can be recovered as part of objectives and subsequently turned in for compensation from Search and Rescue Agents.
It can be valuable to investigate megaships present within a system, to check whether they are subject to a crisis which requires assistance from a sympathetic pilot.

Nonhuman Signal Sources Nonhuman signal sources are locations where xeno activity has been detected. Evacuation procedures may have occurred, leaving escape pods ready to be recovered. These locations can be highly dangerous, so extreme caution is advised before initiating rescue operations at these sites.

Space salvage refers to the retrieval of cargo with a ship. This is accomplished with either a cargo scoop or collector limpets. 

Starport mission boards will occasionally provide Recovery missions to retrieve salvage, both legal and illegal. Sometimes these missions will necessitate the use of an SRV to collect salvage from a planet's surface

Illegal cargo will incur fines or bounties if discovered within a ship's hold. See the Trade and Smuggling guide for information on transporting illegal cargo.

Finding Salvage The primary source of salvage will be signal sources. Whether using the Full Spectrum System Scanner $BINDING_input_either:#value=ExplorationFSSEnter; or by travelling through a system, signal sources will become visible. Pilots can then assess if the signal is worth investigating further, and what level of threat is likely to be encountered. The following signal types are of interest to a salvage pilot:

• Combat Aftermath: Often indicates a ship debris field, where manufactured materials can be recovered. • Degraded Emissions: Indicates ship destruction, with commodities and manufactured materials possibly found within the debris. • Encoded Emissions: May contain a debris field containing common, standard or rare materials which can be recovered. • High-Grade Emissions: Often contain rare or very rare manufactured goods for salvage. • Debris Field: A persistent point of interest containing ship debris. • Salvageable Wreck: Frequently contains cargo for salvage and rescue missions. • Weak Signal Source: Commonly contains illegal cargo dumped by a ship.
codex_pilotshandbook_salvage_rescue_unlo: Search and Rescue Agents Search and Rescue Agents will offer monetary rewards in exchange for recovered pilots, personal belongings or evidence from destroyed craft. These agents are located in the Contacts function of starport services. The items requested by Search and Rescue Agents include the following:

• Black Boxes
• Occupied Escape Pods
• Damaged Escape Pods
• Personal Effects
• Wreckage Components
• Hostages
Black Market Illegal salvage cargo must be sold on the black market. Some starports will host a contact providing access to this marketplace, where illegal goods can be sold.

The price of items on the black market can vary, depending on the goods being traded and the demands of the system. Black market traders take a percentage on the sale of all illegal goods, but all credits earned from stolen cargo is 100% profit.

Stations which feature a black market can be found in the galaxy map via the following method:

• Open the Galaxy Map from the External interface panel • Select the Map Mode tab • Choose the Services overlay from the provided options • Select Black Market from the list of services presented • Systems with black markets will now be highlighted on the map

Carrying illegal goods is risky. System authorities will often scan the manifest of passing ships to check if illegal goods are present. If discovered, a pilot carrying such goods will be issued with a fine or bounty.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_access_: Settlements usually have at least one landing pad available for use by visiting ships and shuttles. Pilots on approach need to request docking permission from the settlement command centre before touching down on a pad.
If no landing pads are available, it is possible to land nearby and travel to the settlement by foot or SRV. No permission is required to land outside a settlement.

Just like planetary ports, settlements operate a no-fire zone in their airspace. Violating settlement laws, or taking hostile actions, will provoke a defensive response from any available anti-air and point defence turrets.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_authori: Settlements utilise an authority system to restrict access to certain areas and functions.

Certain missions will provide a specific authority level to the contractor, allowing them to navigate a settlement as part of the assigned task. But in some situations it is necessary to either obtain or circumvent these security checks. There are three primary ways to do this:

Using an E-Breach to hack into a console will bypass the authority check. An E-Breach only bypasses the authority check of the target console. Once used, an E-Breach cannot be recovered and may be noticed by security.

The Energlink tool allows the user to unleash a surge of energy into a charge port, overloading a nearby console. This is particularly useful for opening security-restricted airlocks. Once a console has been overloaded it cannot be repaired and may be noticed by security. See the Energylink page of the Suit Tools handbook article for more information.

All three of these bypass methods is considered illegal, and penalties will be incurred for exploiting any of them. If the desired authority level cannot be legitimately obtained then it would be wise to keep suspicious actions hidden from settlement personnel.

It is possible to clone the security profile of another individual with the Profile Analyser tool, granting you the associated authority level. The cloned authority works across the whole settlement. See the Profile Analyser page of the Suit Tools handbook article for more information.

Certain rooms within a settlement may be listed as a restricted area. These are marked with holographic banners. Only members of the settlement’s faction are permitted to enter these areas. Trespassers will incur penalties if spotted in a restricted area for any reason, regardless of their authority level.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_buildin: COMMAND CENTRE The administrative hub of a settlement. Controls a settlement’s turrets, alarms and primary data storage.

This section provides a list of the major building types found in various settlements. Note that not all buildings are present at all settlements, as they are constructed depending on the settlement’s purpose.
HABITAT While rarely permanent residences for personnel, settlements usually offer facilities to relax, shower and sleep.
INFIRMARY Buildings providing medical care for personnel. Dedicated medbays are also useful for certain research projects such as pharmaceutical trials.
POWER CENTRE Power centres contain a reactor that supplies power to all settlement buildings. See the Settlement Power page for more information.

PRODUCTION Production buildings house the manufacturing operations of a settlement. The processes involved are dependent on the settlement type. See the Settlement Production page for more information.
STORAGE Warehouses used to store the goods and resources used by the settlement.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_console: SETTLEMENT ALARMS Sets the status of the settlement alarm system to enabled or disabled. Triggered alarms can be switched off via this console.
ANTI-PERSONNEL TURRETS Sets the operational status of the anti-personnel security turrets. When active, these turrets will fire at any individuals hostile to the settlement’s controlling faction.

ATMOSPHERE PROCESSING CONSOLE Controls the artificial atmosphere of a building. Flushing the atmosphere will extinguish any fires and force all inhabitants to use their suit’s life support system to breathe. The atmosphere can be rebuilt using the same console.

AUTHORISATION SCANS Enables or disables the authority checks placed on airlocks. While disabled, airlocks will open for everybody seeking to enter a building. Note that powered airlocks will always open for people seeking to exit a building, regardless of authority.

This section lists all consoles found at a settlement along with their function, except for the power centre and production unit consoles (see their respective pages for information). Many of these require an elevated authority level to operate.
POINT DEFENCE SYSTEM Sets the operational status of the point defence system. When active, these turrets will fire at any missiles fired by hostile forces in the vicinity of the settlement.
ANTI-SHIP TURRETS Sets the operational status of the anti-ship defence turrets. When active, these turrets will fire at any ships hostile to the settlement’s controlling faction.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_contain: Containers provide consumable items or the ability to restock an existing supply. They are typically available for everyone to use, including guests. There are four common container types providing medkits, energy cells, ammunition and grenades.
A wide variety of items can be located in a settlement. While most of these are secure behind locked containers.

Lockers contain goods. These are typically protected by either a maglock strip or a keycode lock. Without a good reason to take an item (such as for a mission objective),  goods are usually considered the property of the settlement’s controlling faction, and taking them will be considered stealing.
Keycodes are displayed to authorised users in the Facilities section of a settlement terminal.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_datapor: Data ports provide a local connection to the settlement’s data network.

Data can be transferred between the port and your suit’s data bank. Each selected file takes time to transfer; the more data, the longer the transfer time. Moving away from the data port before this transfer is completed will pause the transfer. This paused transfer will cancel after a while if you do not return to the data port.

When interfacing with a data port,  select the data you wish to copy to your suit databank before confirming the transfer. To upload data, simply select it for transfer from your databank before confirming.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_introdu: Humanity achieved a long-held dream in the year 2151, with the colonisation of the Tau Ceti system. The first hyperdrive made possible what science-fiction tales had described for centuries: a permanent colony outside of Sol.

But not all colonies are created with the intent of providing a new home. Most surface operations are primarily economical, smaller in scale than planetary ports, offering both access to local resources and employment to those willing to work in a low-atmosphere environment. These locations are collectively known as <font color='#f8f8f8'>settlements.</font>
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_power_d: Power centres are a vital part of settlement operations. These buildings contain a fusion reactor that supplies power to the rest of the settlement.
Thanks to modular technology, power centres are simple to bring online or offline via the power regulator.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_power_p: These modules are vital for the safe operation of a power centre, autonomously managing energy output and reacting to fluctuations. Reactors are designed to shut down if the power regulator is removed, and will only activate when one is present.
When the regulator housing is open, players can take or place a regulator as needed. Regulators are stored in a suit backpack when carried.
While a settlement has no power the following status changes occur:

- Consoles and airlocks are inoperable. Individual consoles and airlocks can be powered up with the energylink tool.
- Alarms are disabled.
- Restricted areas are no longer defined.
- Settlement defences are disabled.
- Data points and recharge sockets are inactive.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_powerso: These ports receive energy from an external source. Charge ports are typically attached to a mechanism, such as an airlock. If a settlement is offline, charge ports can be used to power that specific mechanism by transferring energy from your suit battery via the energylink tool.

These sockets are often kept secure behind maintenance panels. Accessing them will require the <font color='#f8f8f8'>arc cutter</font> tool. See the Arc Cutter page of the Suit Tools handbook article for more information.
There are two types of power socket located in various settlement buildings: <font color='#f8f8f8'>charge ports</font> and <font color='#f8f8f8'>suit recharge sockets</font>.

As suggested by the name, recharge sockets supply power. Suit batteries can be recharged at these sockets via the energylink tool. See the Energylink page of the Suit Tools handbook article for more information.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_precis: A guide to settlement features and navigation.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_settlem: Some settlements contain production buildings that manufacture goods or commodities. These are generally found in agricultural, extraction or industrial settlements.
Production buildings have two unique machines within:

Production units oversee an important aspect of a settlement’s manufacturing process. Ingredients can be added to that process via these units. Depending on the settlement type, these units are named as follows:

- Environmental Regulation Unit (Agricultural)
- Catalyst Management Unit (Extraction)
- Synthesis Automation Unit (Industrial)
These units contain a specific sample of the settlement’s production process. Used for quality control checks or refinement of the current processes, these samples can be withdrawn at any time.

An elevated authority level is usually required to open these units. Using a unit’s console will trigger a settlement alarm regardless of the operator’s authority level. Opening a settlement’s production units when not a registered member of the owning faction will incur penalties.
AGRICULTURE Focused on the production of food or other valuable crops, these settlements employ modern hydroponic technology to cultivate plants in environmentally controlled enclosures.
A settlement typically falls under one of the following categories based on its intended purpose.

EXTRACTION Designed to exploit sub-surface resources, these settlements establish huge mining rigs to carve deep below a planet’s surface. The exposed minerals are then extracted and prepared for export.
INDUSTRIAL These settlements are manufacturing hubs, turning raw resources and components into goods. Productions buildings and storage silos are the primary identifying features.

MILITARY Fortified settlements used as staging posts for military operations. They typically include more defensive turrets than most settlements and provide barracks and armouries to accommodate combatants.
RESEARCH Dedicated to the advancement of science and technology, these settlements provide laboratory space and equipment for researchers. Telescope arrays are common at these sites.
TOURISM Frequented by workers and pilots who require a break from space travel. Tourism settlements offer a bar to unwind in and sleeping quarters for the weary, among other amenities.
codex_pilotshandbook_settlements_termina: CONNECTION SUMMARY Displays your current authority level, the operational status of the settlement and the location of the current terminal.
Settlement terminals provide information about all the available buildings, rooms and objects. You can set an Insight marker on these to help locate them.
The sections of a settlement terminal are as follows:

FACILITIES Shows all locations and objects. Buildings are listed as tabs on the left side of the panel. Selecting a building will bring up all rooms found within it. Highlighting a room will list all objects within; this includes containers, data ports, terminals and consoles.
If you have acquired a locked container keycode, that keycode will be displayed in the object list beside the container it applies to.

MISSION BOARD Lists all available missions for the current settlement. Missions can be filtered by category and reward type. The primary difference between settlement and starport mission boards is that settlements only offer missions from the owning faction.
STAFF LIST Provides a full list of all personnel registered at the settlement. This includes their name, job title, faction allegiance, combat rank and authority clearance.
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_cons: This section provides an overview of the available single-use consumables.
E-BREACH - Hacks into console security software, bypassing the need for an authority profile. The use of an E-Breach is illegal and will incur a bounty if witnessed.
ENERGY CELL - A portable medical kit used to restore the user’s health.
FRAG GRENADE - A manually thrown explosive that damages nearby targets.
MEDKIT - A portable medical kit used to restore the user’s health.
SHIELD DISRUPTOR - Disrupts nearby shields for a short time when deployed.
SHIELD PROJECTOR - Generates a shield barrier once deployed which is capable of absorbing damage.
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_func: AIR Should a suit run out of energy, the life support system will offer a limited amount of air. You must locate a pressurised environment or vehicle, or some means of recharging the suit battery, before asphyxiation occurs.
BACKPACK - Provides inventory space for various goods, assets and data. Ammunition and consumables also have a capacity limit per type.
All suits have two main resources: Energy and Air.
Suits also come with the following core modules:

ENERGY Suit batteries are a core module and hold a finite energy supply. Whenever operating outside of a pressurised building or vehicle, the energy supply will slowly deplete as it maintains the life support module that keeps the wearer breathing. Energy is also spent on maintaining shields and when powering mechanisms with the Energylink tool.
Suit energy can be recovered with <font color='#f8f8f8'>energy cells</font>, or at <font color='#f8f8f8'>recharge sockets</font> by using the energylink tool.
FLASHLIGHT - Illuminates dark areas. Can be toggled on or off as needed.

JUMP ASSIST - Allows the wearer to jump higher and further using a thrust-assisted module on the suit’s back. While offering greater versatility when traversing a planet’s surface, the jump assist module should not be considered an alternate form of flight as the thrust it offers per charge is minimal.
LIFE SUPPORT - Supplies air to the wearer in unpressurised environments. The suit helmet will automatically deploy or retract when passing between pressurised and unpressurised areas.
SENSORS - Scans the surrounding area passively, and are used for orientation and the tracking of objects/targets via compass and radar displays.

SHIELD GENERATOR - Projects a personal shield around the wearer, capable of absorbing incoming attacks. Drains the suit battery while active. If the shield is depleted by incoming attacks it will take time to regenerate them.
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_insi: Displays a wide range of information related to your progress and information about the galaxy. This includes:

- Your current CMDR status
- Galnet News
- Engineer progress (See the Engineers guide for more information)
- The Squadrons interface
- The Powerplay interface
- The Codex hub
UP - COMMS Accesses the Comms panel. This allows communication via multiple channels, offers access to your inbox messages, and additional social options.
This section explores the options available in the Insight wheel.
The Insight Hub contains a wealth of information displayed via your suit’s HUD. This is designed to replicate the information at a Commander’s disposal when viewing a ship’s cockpit interface panels.
By bringing up the Insight wheel, you have four navigational choices:
LEFT - EXTERNAL INTERFACE Offers several panels similar to those provided in a ship’s cockpit. These include:

- Navigation Panel, for viewing local contacts, setting waypoints and accessing your galaxy, system and planetary maps. - Transactions Panel, to display your active missions, vouchers and outstanding legal warrants. - Contacts Panel, which lists all known contacts in the area. - Apex App, allowing shuttle booking from the current location. You must be inside the human bubble, within the fuel range of a shuttle, and in a safe location (excluding ports). See the Apex Interstellar page of the Concourse guide for more information.
DOWN - INVENTORY Brings up your backpack’s contents and related inventory.
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_intr: Ever since Yuri Gagarin ventured into Earth’s orbit wearing the SK-1 suit, humanity has sought to develop more practical and efficient suits to protect them from the hazards of space exploration. The bulky designs of early spaceflight have been left far behind; modern space suits are sleek, effective garments.

Different suits are typically tailored to fulfil a particular role. Most can be accessorised and upgraded, even modified by specialist engineers. But there are many basic requirements and rules for every suit. Understanding how a suit functions is vital for achieving your objectives…and staying alive in dangerous situations.
Suits and other personal equipment can be purchased at any Pioneer Supplies vendor, found in all starports.
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_item: All interactive suit tools, modules and consumables can be selected via the item wheel.

Highlighting an option and releasing the item wheel will equip, use or toggle the selection, depending on context. The following options are available, starting at the top of the wheel and working clockwise:

- Frag Grenade (Equip)
- Shield Disruptor (Equip)
- Medkit (Use)
- Night Vision (Toggle On/Off)
- Shield (Toggle On/Off)
- Flashlight (Toggle On/Off)
- Energy Cell (Use)
- Shield Projector (Equip)
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_prec: A guide covering suit, weapon and tool functionality.
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_purc: Suits and other personal equipment can be purchased at any Pioneer Supplies vendor, <font color='#f8f8f8'>found in all starports.</font>
codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_suit: <font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>ARC CUTTER</font>
Maverick Suit
The arc cutter emits a high-strength, concentrated beam of energy used to cut through physical objects such as maintenance panels and maglocks.
This tool has a single Cut mode. The tool has a safety feature that only permits the beam to fire when aiming at a suitable object.
Using the arc cutter to carve open faction property is an illegal act, and being observed doing so will incur penalties.
<font size='40'>SUIT TOOLS - ARC CUTTER</font>
<font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>ENERGYLINK TOOL</font>
All Suits

The energylink facilitates the transfer of energy between a suit battery and either a charge port or a recharge socket. It can also be used to power mechanisms when navigating an offline facility. Transferring energy from your suit to a charge port will consume a portion of your suit energy.
The energylink comes with two modes:

OVERLOAD MODE When triggered, this mode will transfer a burst of energy to a charge port, causing a surge of electricity that will overload the associated mechanism. This allows the user to bypass authority checks for airlocks. Once overloaded, a device will remain out of commission. Overload mode can also be used as an attack, sending a surge of energy through the target’s suit.
It is illegal to carry an energylink in Overload mode, overload a mechanism, or assault someone with the tool. Being observed committing any of these acts will incur penalties.
<font size='40'>SUIT TOOLS - ENERGYLINK</font>
TRANSFER MODE When triggered, this mode transfers power between your suit battery and the target receptacle.

codex_pilotshandbook_suitsequipment_weap: CARBINES Primary Weapon - Compact automatic weapons designed to unleash bursts at short range.
This section provides an overview of hand-held weaponry that requires ammunition.
Weapons fire kinetic, laser, plasma or explosive projectiles depending on the model used.
LONG RANGE RIFLES Primary Weapon - Slowly operated scoped rifle that delivers high damage from long range.
PISTOLS Secondary Weapon - A lightweight firearm, useful at short range but lacking in power.
RIFLES Primary Weapon - A long-barrelled automatic firearm, typically offering a high rate of fire and decent range.
SHOTGUNS Primary Weapon - Semi-automatic weapons capable of extensive damage at close range.

Personal weapon types follow the same basic functionality as ship hardpoints. All personal weapons require ammunition to fire. Ammunition is replenished by ammunition boxes or when entering a vehicle.

EXPLOSIVE WEAPONS Personal explosive weapons are designed for effectiveness in both pressurised and unpressurised scenarios, using pressure waves and fragmentation to tear through enemies. Personal launchers use dumbfire projectiles.
KINETIC WEAPONS Kinetic weapons are the most efficient means of penetrating a target's armour but are less effective against shields.

THERMAL WEAPONS Thermal laser weapons are the most effective means of stripping away shields but are less successful against armour. A common tactic is to deploy thermal weapons to remove a target's shield before switching to a kinetic weapon.
Unlike thermal hardpoints, personal weapons do not automatically recharge over time and must be loaded with battery clips.

THERMAL-KINETIC WEAPONS Thermal-kinetic plasma weapons are capable of dealing damage to both shields and armour. They are reliable all-purpose weapons, though lacking the specific effectiveness of kinetic or thermal firearms.
codex_pilotshandbook_systemcolonisation_: System Colonisation construction efforts can be found via the Galaxy Map. Selecting these construction efforts will show the list of remaining resources required to complete it. By delivering these resources commanders will aid in the construction effort. These construction efforts pay above the galactic average for each commodity delivered and so are a great and reliable way to trade in bulk.
<font size='40'>AIDING A SYSTEM COLONISATION EFFORT</font>

Claims allow a faction to expand from an inhabited system into a uninhabited one. These claims are placed on systems chosen by commanders and paid for by them. Once the claim has been completed the commander then takes on the role of System Architect.

All System Colonisation efforts start from a System Colonisation Contact, these can be found in most ports and allow commanders to expand to an uninhabited system within range. System Contacts give information about ongoing claims, such as the stage of the claim and how to proceed.
Once a system is selected the Primary Port can be configured. Each Port type provides different benefits to the system and requires varying amounts of commodities to be delivered to complete.
Upon selection a System Colonisation Beacon will be assigned, and must be deployed via the System Colonisation Suite internal module to the designated location around the primary star.

Delivery must be completed within 24 hours of making the claim or it will be revoked. No refund will be offered but commanders may attempt the claim again or attempt to claim a different system. Should a claim fail to complete on the same system for a second time that system will not be claimable by the same commander for a number of days.
<font size='40'>CLAIMS</font>

Facilities which have markets but do not start with a specific economy will derive one based on the body the market is on or orbiting. Some of these characteristics can combine, for example, a Rocky Body with Rings will have both Refinery and Extraction economies.

Body:

All Other Stars - Military

<font size='40'>Economy Overrides</font>

Facilities are structures, complexes, stations, installations and settlements built within a system. Each facility has a different list of resources required for its construction, though many resources are shared between facilities.

There are 3 different Tiers of facility, each will produce and/or consume Construction Points. Tiers 1 and 2 produce Tier 2 and 3 Construction Points respectively when completed and Tier 2 and 3 Facilities consume these Construction Points when selected for construction.

Some facilities have prerequisites that require another facility to already be built within the system before they can be chosen for construction. These prerequisites are shown when selecting a slot and viewing a facility for construction.

Each facility constructed provides bonuses to the system such as increasing the population, tech level, security, wealth and standard of living, these bonuses are listed when selecting a facility for construction.

Facilities can influence the economy of markets around and on the local body. This results in the market being more likely to produce commodities that relate to the economy, for example an agricultural settlement will influence markets to produce food products such as grain and Tea.

The statistics of commodities produced by a market depend on the population of the market, the higher the markets population the more commodities will be produced. Market population is determined by the market type and facilities nearby that boost population.

System statistics are influenced by facilities this includes: Security, Tech Level, Wealth, Standard of Living and Development Level. Facilities will mostly increase one or more of these statistics, but some can decrease them as well.
<font size='40'>FACILITIES</font>
System Colonisation
The 34th century has seen humanity stagnate in its expansion efforts. With the close of the 2nd Thargoid War Humanity finds itself in urgent need of new territory.

Factions throughout human space are looking for Commanders to help drive System Colonisation ventures. Commanders will be given the opportunity to guide the development of these new territories, select the major facilities and establish system economies.
<font size='40'>INTRODUCTION</font>
Weak Links:

Supporting facilities, such as a Settlement, create Weak Links to all Ports within the System that are not on the same planetary body, or within the same orbit. These supporting economies provide small boosts to those Ports, affecting all equally.
Strong Links:

A Strong Link is formed between a facility that produces an economy and a single Port on or orbiting the same body. These links provide a larger economic boost to a connected market. Ports on a planetary surface will pass these links to a Port orbiting the same body, whilst retaining the benefits for themselves.
Strong Links follow a priority system where multiple Markets exist.

- Ports in the same relative location, whether in orbit or on the surface, will receive priority over the other, i.e. Supporting Facilities on a planet’s surface will prioritise a surface Port over an orbital one.

- If a Tier 1 Port exists with Strong Links, and a further Tier 2 Port is built in the same relative location, then those Strong Links will be redirected to the new Tier 2 market. The Tier 1 market will additionally begin to support this new market.
- If a Tier 2 Port exists with Strong Links, and a further Tier 1 Port is built in the same relative location, then the Tier 1 will simply support the Tier 2 without taking over its Strong Link.
- If two Markets of the same Tier exist in the same relative location, then the first built will retain the Strong Link.
<font size='40'>MARKET LINKS</font>
Markets exist wherever a commander can trade commodities. A market’s strength is determined by a System’s associated Population size, Characteristics and supporting Economies.

Ports include Outposts, Coriolis, Orbis, Ocellus Stations, Asteroid Bases, and Planetary Ports, and offer extensive trading options and can supply a larger volume and variety of commodities if adequately supported.

Supporting facilities are any facilities that supply a Port with a market economy. These can include Settlements, Installations and Hubs. Their primary function is to support commodity trading of the Port’s economy. Ports can also act as Supporting Facilities under certain conditions.

Markets can benefit from multiple economy types simultaneously. The strength of an economy determines the supply of commodities available; the stronger the economy, the more quantity of a given commodity is produced.
<font size='40'>MARKETS</font>

Population size associated with a Market within a System affects the availability of commodities and their supply. The higher the Population, the greater the Supply. To achieve significant increases in available Supply requires an exponential increase in Population growth.
<font size='40'>SYSTEM POPULATION</font>
An introduction to engaging with System Colonisation.

After deployment of the System Colonisation Beacon a System Colonisation Ship will jump to the Primary Port's construction location allowing for the delivery of resources to complete construction. Resources for the primary star port include additional commodities needed to support the infrastructure for future system development.
Should the Primary Port construction fail to be completed within the designated time the System Colonisation effort will fail and all commodities delivered up to that point will be lost.
<font size='40'>PRIMARY PORT</font>

When the Primary Port has been completed the commander who funded the System Colonisation effort becomes the System Architect for the newly settled system.

System Architects can use the Architect view mode in the system map to view locations where facilities can be placed. This view also allows selection of construction sites to choose a facilities to build. These construction efforts work the same as the Primary Port except they have no time limit. Only a certain number of construction projects can be active at one time in a system, as facilities are completed this number increases up to a maximum.

The location of facilities placed in orbit and the type of facility to be created is performed directly in the architect view. The availability of sites on planetary bodies is shown in the architect view but to place the facility the architect must travel to the body and manually select and position the facility using the Colonisation Suite internal module.

codex_pilotshandbook_theconcourse_introd: With many modern professions demanding interstellar travel, the concourse offers a peaceful refuge from the many challenges found in deep space. Each day combat pilots, traders, researchers and more pass through this area, which is exempt from the more involved customs checks of local residential areas.

Equipment, vouchers, goods and more can be traded at various establishments. Those looking for work will easily find it too, as both individuals offering contracts and the terminal mission board supply a wide variety of tasks.
codex_pilotshandbook_theconcourse_pionee: With a wide range of suits, firearms and other equipment perfect for field operations, Pioneer Supplies is popular with mercenaries, explorers and contractors of all types. codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_ca: Standard Commodities Your regular cargo for trade on the commodities market. Most commodities can be bought at a market, while some must be mined or collected as salvage. A handful of goods are only produced on planet surfaces.

Rare Goods Rare goods are commodities produced by a single location only, which increase in value based on the distance away from their origin. Unlike other commodities, rare goods are rationed on a per-commander basis.

Prohibited Goods Prohibited goods are illegal in specific jurisdictions, dictated by the ruling minor faction. For example, personal weapons may be traded in a dictatorship, but not in a theocracy. Prohibited goods can only be sold on the black market and you may receive fines or bounties if scanned while carrying them. Pilots travelling through anarchy systems will avoid such scans, and this government type will trade in almost all commodities.

Stolen Goods Stolen goods are those that have been acquired through illegal means. This could be via pirating another ship or abandoning a mission where cargo has been provided. Stolen goods can only be sold on the black market and you may receive fines or bounties if scanned while carrying them. Pilots travelling through anarchy systems will avoid such scans, and this government type will trade in almost all commodities.

Mission Cargo Mission cargo cannot be sold on the commodities market. Abandoning a mission will remove the mission tag from any cargo in your hold but will also mark that cargo as stolen. Abandoning missions can lead to reputation loss and fines.
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_ga: The Galaxy Map has tools allowing a trader to determine which systems supply or demand a particular commodity. The following map overlays provide a number of helpful options when searching for a trade route.
Commodity User Data Tab Select the commodity category in the sub-menu, followed by the specific cargo you're interested in.

State Map Mode Tab This displays system states, denoting where specific trades may be of particular interest to a market. For example, a system currently experiencing an Outbreak will have an elevated need for basic medicines, which will increase the demand – and price - of this commodity.
Economy User Data Tab Filtering for specific economy types helps inform where certain goods may be supplied. For example, Industrial economies will offer many types of consumer items and machinery.
Trending Trade Routes Trade Tools Tab This view shows trades of commodity types occurring in volume and can be filtered to show activity by Commanders or general commercial traffic.

Bright lines, coloured to match their commodity type, will flow from one system to another, denoting that the commodity in question is currently imported into that system. The prominence of a line signifies how busy a trade route is.

While useful for highlighting trade hotspots or new demand/supply links, there may be less profit found at older routes where the demands of the importing system have been met. In addition, pirates often use high volume routes to hunt prospective targets.
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_in: The Inventory tab, shown in the right side panel, displays any commodities currently in the cargo hold. This includes highlighting the quantity, legality in the current system, whether a shipment is stolen and the galactic average cost. A selected item offers additional details, the option to discard or jettison cargo, and a link to the galaxy map which will offer the price of that commodity in systems where you have logged trade data.
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_pr: A guide to trading, even outside the law.
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_se: Smuggled cargo must be sold on the black market. Some starports will host a contact providing access to this marketplace, where stolen or prohibited goods can be sold.

The price of items on the black market can vary, depending on the goods being traded and the demands of the system. Black market traders take a percentage on the sale of all stolen goods, but all credits made on stolen cargo is 100% profit.
Stations which feature a black market can be found in the galaxy map via the following method:

• Open the Galaxy Map from the External interface panel • Select the User Data View tab • Choose the Services option from the presented menu • Select Black Market from the list of services • Systems with black markets will now be highlighted on the map

Carrying stolen goods is risky. System authorities will often scan the manifest of passing ships to check if stolen/prohibited goods are present. If discovered, a pilot carrying such goods will be issued with a fine or bounty.
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_si: Silent running $BINDING_input_either:#value=TOGGLEBUTTONUPINPUT; is the term used for minimising a ship's heat signature drastically for a limited period. It is particularly useful when approaching a station, to help minimise the range in which system authorities can scan a ship's cargo manifest.
Silent running can also be toggled in the Functions tab.
In this mode, a ship will deactivate shields and all heat vents will close completely. This severely reduces heat emissions, making a ship particularly hard to detect on scanners.

The trade-off is the build-up of heat inside of the ship, raising the temperature. Eventually this heat will begin to impact modules, causing damage and malfunctions in response to high temperatures. It is advisable not to utilise silent running for too long. The heatsink launcher can help you manage the heat build-up by ejecting heat during use.
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_sm: <font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>CARGO RACK</font>
<font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>HEATSINK LAUNCHER</font>
<font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>COLLECTOR LIMPET CONTROLLER</font>
CARGO RACK Optional Internal
Provides storage space for cargo canisters, allowing their safe transportation. The number of cargo units held in each rack is determined by the class of each rack.
HEATSINK LAUNCHER Utility Mount
Ejects heatsinks, rapidly reducing a ship's heat levels. A low-temperature ship is harder to track and scan.
COLLECTOR LIMPET CONTROLLER Optional Internal (various)
Deploys limpets to gather up any nearby cargo canisters and return them to your ship.
<font size='40'>SMUGGLING EQUIPMENT</font>

Smuggling is a form of trade, with one primary difference: the legality of the cargo. A smuggler must rely on stealth, cunning and careful planning to avoid detection when carrying restricted or stolen goods. Fines and bounties will be issued against a pilot discovered carrying illicit cargo.

Commanders can buy illegal cargo on the commodities market, or sell their prohibited or stolen cargo at a black market. They can also find smuggling missions on the mission board. Pilots looking for work via the mission board should pay attention to the following mission types: • Smuggling, in which illegal cargo is provided and must be delivered to a set destination without the cargo being detected.
<font size='40'>SMUGGLING INTRODUCTION</font>
Smugglers have several methods of collecting cargo for transport:

• Accepting smuggling missions, which supply both cargo and a predetermined destination
• Collecting cargo from deep space, wreckages or victims of piracy
• Hauling cargo bought legally from a market into a system where that cargo is prohibited

Cargo canisters can be gathered with collector limpets or via the cargo scoop. Collector limpets are much more efficient but do take up precious space in a ship's loadout and hold. Smuggled cargo is then sold on the black market or handed in to fulfil a mission requirement.
<font size='20' color='#f8f8f8'>HEAT</font>

Smuggling is a lot easier if your ship can't be detected.

All ships produce heat. The temperature of a ship dictates its visibility on ship scanners. Ships which maintain a heat level of under 20% greatly reduce the range at which other ships – including system authorities - can successfully scan them.
The ship's heat is displayed on the left of your radar. Your ship's heat signature is displayed above the fuel bar.

Many modules generate heat when powered, based on a value displayed in the Outfitting screen. As a ship performs certain actions – such as boosting, initiating a hyperspace jump or firing weapons – the collective heat generated by a ship will increase. Upgraded or engineered modules can influence how quickly a ship generates heat. Switching off unnecessary modules will also reduce a ship's thermal output.
<font size='40'>SMUGGLING PROCESS</font>
codex_pilotshandbook_trader_smuggling_tr: Trade forms the backbone of the galactic economy. Typically, traders follow the supply and demand dictated by the commodities market, travelling between systems to buy low and sell high. This simple rule can produce considerable profits – provided any pirates stalking a trade route can be avoided.

Commanders can buy and sell cargo on the commodities market or black market, or contribute cargo to complete missions. Pilots looking for work via the mission board should pay attention to the following mission types: • Delivery, in which cargo is provided and must be delivered to a set destination. • Collection, in which certain commodities must be located, purchased and then delivered to a set destination.
<font size='40'>TRADE INTRODUCTION</font>
<font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>CARGO RACK</font>
<font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>FRAME SHIFT DRIVE</font>
<font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>FUEL SCOOP</font>
CARGO RACK Optional Internal
Provides storage space for cargo canisters, allowing their safe transportation. The number of cargo units held in each rack is determined by the module's class.

Unlike many other careers, trade ship builds are determined by a single primary factor: the cargo hold. Every additional cargo canister a ship can carry per run equals more profit, so a wise trader will look to outfit as many cargo racks as possible.
However, a handful of modules can be upgraded to grant a trader further efficiency gains:
FRAME SHIFT DRIVE Core Internal
Dictates the hyperspace jump range of a ship, meaning a higher rated FSD can reduce the number of jumps when travelling between stations.
FUEL SCOOP Optional Internal
Converts hydrogen collected from a star's corona into usable fuel. Increases a trader's travel range without the need to dock for refuelling.
<font size='40'>TRADING EQUIPMENT</font>
The basic premise of trading is to purchase goods from a market offering them in high supply, and transporting those goods to a market where they are in great demand.

Cargo is bought and sold on the Commodities Market, found on the Starport Services menu. The market has two display modes: • Buy, which highlights the goods offered for purchase at the current market. This screen displays the Demand value of each good. • Sell, which highlights the goods currently required by the current market. This screen displays the Supply value of each good.

A commodity in particularly high supply will be marked with a green icon, and the cost of purchase will typically be lower than the galactic average price. Conversely, stocks in great demand will pay above the galactic average for any units of that commodity delivered to them. The market offers a variety of filters to tailor the display to the trader's needs.

By selecting a particular commodity, pilots can buy or sell cargo as necessary in the pop-up screen; this screen will also show nearby systems that import the commodity and what price the local market trades at. Selecting a displayed market will navigate to the galaxy map to view its location.
Prices are influenced by a variety of factors, such as system states. Illegal items will not be displayed on the commodity market, and will instead need to be sold on the black market.
<font size='40'>TRADING PROCESS</font>

A fully loaded trade ship will have a greater fuel requirement than an empty one. Plotting a route after all required cargo has been purchased will offer a more accurate calculation for route plotting.
It is also possible to view how a full cargo bay adjusts a ship's jump capability by adjusting the Cargo Mass slider.

Trading in anarchy systems brings additional risk, as no system security exists to respond to any distress calls. Due to the lack of local authorities and law, it may be worthwhile forming a wing for additional protection in these systems.
Filling any unused cargo space with commodities when performing missions can provide a nice addition to a pilot's income.
In larger ships, trading a personal quota of rare goods can be a profitable enterprise if picked up alongside a bulk shipment of standard commodities.
Cargo is not covered by ship insurance, so retaining the funds necessary to replace a forfeit payload is important.

Finding a multi-stop route can be more efficient than a two-system import/export relationship. Traders may plot a chain of markets supplying each other, looping around to the original location to begin the cycle again.
Occasionally, traders opt to carry a small quantity of low-value cargo to be jettisoned when attempting to discourage a pirate attack, or alternatively to buy time for an escape.
<font size='40'>TRADING TIPS</font>
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_advequip: Combining human and Guardian technology, these hybrid weapons are effective against both human and Thargoid craft. The blueprints for these weapons must first be acquired from a Technology Broker before they can be purchased. For more information on the Guardians, please refer to the related topic available in the Codex.
Increases the number of experimental weapon hardpoints a ship can outfit at one time.
Offers protection from the massive energy surges found inside Thargoid Maelstroms.
Draws caustic elements away from the ship's hull and into an ejectable container, prolonging ship survival in caustic environments.
Fires a high-velocity projectile effective at penetrating armour, similar to a standard rail gun. This hardpoint counts towards a ship's experimental weapon limit.
Generates a ball of plasma from a stream controlled manually by the player, influence the potency of the projectile. This hardpoint counts towards a ship's experimental weapon limit.
Launches multiple projectiles, causing high damage at short range. This hardpoint counts towards a ship's experimental weapon limit.
CORROSION RESISTANT CARGO RACK Optional Internal
Allows the safe storage of corrosive Thargoid objects without risk of damage to the ship.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_assistan: Xeno hunters have other, more humanitarian avenues for countering the fallout of Thargoid attacks. Often civilians will need to be evacuated to safer areas, but accomplishing this can be a hazardous task.

Capital Class Ships / Megaships Megaships and capital ships have been known to face Thargoid attack. During such an encounter, these huge vessels may call upon nearby Commanders to help defend them, repair the damage they have sustained, or evacuate personnel to safety.

Damaged Starports Starports and planetary ports in systems facing Thargoid invasion are likely to be damaged by Thargoid attacks. Civilians and starport personnel will need to be evacuated, but the interior of a damaged starport is a volatile environment. Ships undertaking rescue missions require heatsink launchers to avoid taking damage in the fierce temperatures generated inside a burning station. Passenger ships will carry refugees, but some in need of evacuation will be stored in escape pods for transport in a ship's hold. Ports that are either under attack or burning from a prior attack will request emergency supplies, which can be delivered to the ports from other locations. Black boxes and occupied escape pods can be found in systems with a Thargoid presence. These need to be collected and returned to a safe location, such as Rescue Megaships. Counterstrike Systems Marked in the Galaxy map (unless filtered), these represent Thargoid-controlled systems which have been targeted for counter-offensive operations. Sustained conflict zones around abandoned ports, and an expanded range of activities, will help human forces to reclaim these systems. Rescue Megaship Rescue ships will be established at specific locations considered safe from the Thargoid fleet's advance. These massive craft will act as the focal point for evacuation efforts. They also offer standard AX weaponry for pilots needing to outfit their vessels before joining the war effort. If a port containing a Commander's stored craft is destroyed by Thargoids, the craft will be automatically transferred to the nearest rescue ship.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_basicequ: Perhaps more than any other profession, xeno hunting requires a ship to be properly outfitted prior to seeking out Thargoid opponents. The primary reason for this is the fact that standard weaponry has proven ineffective against Thargoid ships, and early military engagements were distinctly one-sided.

Thanks to the efforts of Aegis, a research initiative created by the three galactic superpowers, technology to counter the Thargoid threat was developed in the early stages of the war.  Weaponry is available to purchase in systems with high tech, military, industrial and refinery economies. 

Only <font size='16' color='#f8f8f8'>4</font> experimental AX weapons can be fitted to a vessel by default.

Launches dumbfire missiles which explode with a compound designed to damage alien ships. Missiles are commonly used to force Thargoid Interceptors to expose their vulnerable 'heart' components. This hardpoint counts towards a ship's experimental weapon limit.

Fires projectiles tipped with a compound designed to damage alien vessels. Multi-cannons, along with some more specialised weapon variants, are effective against the exposed hearts of Thargoid Interceptors. This hardpoint counts towards a ship's experimental weapon limit. 

Enhanced versions of these two weapons are available at rescue megaships, providing increased damage output.
Releases flak rounds designed to counter alien swarming technology such as Thargons. Can be manually detonated. This hardpoint does not count towards a ship's experimental weapon limit.
Note that AX weapons are less effective against human ships than regular weaponry.
Creates interference that neutralises the shutdown field emitted by alien craft. Drains the current SYS charge while active.

Scans xeno-biological vessels, providing both basic craft information and detailed sub-target information and statistical data. 

An enhanced version of this scanner with increased range is also available.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_introduc: Ever since the return of the fearsome alien race known as the Thargoids in 3303, humanity's need for Commanders to fight back has continued to grow. The risks are great, and aspiring xeno hunters will need specialised weaponry and a strong understanding of combat operations to succeed. The rewards are high, however, and combat with the Thargoids is a thrilling experience for those who survive. Pilots looking for xeno hunting work via the mission board should pay attention to the following mission types: • Thargoid Combat, in which pilots are tasked with locating and destroying Thargoid vessels of a set class. These are typically found in systems with the Thargoid Alert and Invasion states.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_locateth: There are several methods of locating Thargoids in a star system.

Nonhuman Signal Sources (NHSS) Whether through the Full Spectrum System Scanner $BINDING_input_either:#value=ExplorationFSSEnter; or by simply travelling through a system, Commanders may come across a Nonhuman Signal Source (NHSS). This denotes a source of alien origin, likely indicating one or more Thargoid vessels. The ship's computer will evaluate signals to assign a threat level. The higher the threat level, the greater the estimated danger.

AX Conflict Zones With the recent escalation of the Thargoid War, multiple human systems have seen a surge in alien activity. Anti-xeno conflict zones will commonly be seen in systems with a Thargoid presence, and pilots are encouraged to join these fights - provided their ship is equipped for such! - and help repel the alien fleet.

Thargoid Engagement Thargoids have reportedly been seeking out human ships travelling through star systems in which the aliens are active. Hyperdictions - where ships are torn out of a hyperspace jump - are common between systems with a Thargoid presence. There are also been multiple verified reports that human ships dropping out of FSD travel modes will draw attention from alien craft in these system. Pay close attention to your radar and ship computer notifications, and stay alert for incoming energy surges.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_precis: A guide to fighting the xeno menace that threatens our galaxy.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_surfaces: Thargoids have established a presence on many worlds since discovered by humans. Initial assessments of these sites have provided a broad overview of the key features of each, but the true nature of these locations may never be known. Still, they offer a tantalising opportunity to experience how the Thargoid race organises its forward surface operations.

Surface Sites Huge imprints in the ground suggests the outline of an ancient Thargoid mothership. Some of these ruins can be entered while carrying a Thargoid Probe or Sensor. Active surface sites have a functional device in their central chamber which can be activated with a set of one Thargoid Link, Probe and Sensor. Doing so produces a star map projection on the chamber ceiling. Research by Professor Ishmael Palin and Ram Tah in 3308 revealed that inserting a Guardian Relic into this central device will generate an unclassified relic comprising both Thargoid and Guardian elements. All other Guardian objects invoke a violent response. The areas are patrolled by Scavenger drones, which are not hostile unless antagonised.

Spire Sites These sprawling areas suggest some kind of industrial operation on the surface of worlds which are alien to the Thargoid’s preferred ammonia atmospheres. They are found almost exclusively within a 30LY radius of a Thargoid Titan. Little is known about these areas for the moment, and exploration of these areas is important – though dangerous. Deadly combat drones like the Revenant sweep the area while Scouts and Interceptors patrol the skies. But such defensive measures suggest that the spire sites are considered important by the Thargoid fleet.
codex_pilotshandbook_xenohunter_thargoid: The Thargoids are an ancient insectoid race of uncertain origin. Study of Thargoid technology suggests that their ships are at least partly organic, with biomechanical 'hearts' of varying numbers found within. Larger vessels are capable of interdicting human ships travelling through hyperspace. More recently, Thargoids have congregated in great numbers to attack entire systems, leaving human stations and fleets in ruins.
• Glaives, which are extremely fast and highly aggressive combat vessels. • Scythes, which prioritise the abduction of humans using hull-breaching chemical weapons and collector drones.

THARGOID VESSELS Thargoid Interceptors Large, powerful vessels armed with a variety of offensive and defensive capabilities. They are capable of releasing swarms of drones called Thargons to attack and disorientate their targets. Four known variants of Interceptor are ranked by increasing power; these have been classed as:

Thargoid Scouts Small ships that attack in numbers. They are armed with energy weapons and caustic missiles. Scouts can be damaged with conventional weaponry, unlike the larger Interceptors. There are four known variants of Scout, each with different capabilities:

• Marauders, the standard Scout craft. • Berserkers, a more dangerous Scout which releases a pulse periodically, releasing a number of caustic missiles and increasing the damage output of any nearby Scouts. • Inciters, which increase the speed and agility of nearby Scouts. • Regenerators, which releases a pulse that heals nearby Scouts.

Rewards Each confirmed Thargoid kill earns a bounty voucher for a significant credit value. These can be cashed in at any station. Other items, commodities and resources may also be salvaged from defeated Thargoid vessels.
A fifth additional variant acts in a more logistical capacity, often encountered in advance of a Thargoid invasion fleet:
Thargoid Hunters Medium-sized ships used in more specialised roles than the Interceptors and Scouts which constitute the bulk of Thargoid forces. There are currently two known variants of Hunter:

The Second Thargoid War started in 3303, and has ebbed and flowed with periods of escalation and relative dormancy. In recent times, however, Thargoid aggression has increased considerably.

It now seems apparent that the Thargoids have initiated a full-scale invasion of human space. Multiple populated systems have reported huge numbers of Thargoids swarming through them, ferociously attacking starports, planetary ports and human fleets. Millions of refugees have been seen fleeing their homes.

It is now up to humanity to react. A series of system states have been identified, which can be filtered for in the Galaxy Map.

Thargoid Alert A system will enter the Alert state when Thargoids have been reported moving through its space, often as a precursor to a broader invasion. Markets in an Alert system will offer missions to hunt down Thargoid ships to prevent an invasion force from establishing a presence.

Thargoid Invasion If a human controlled system is unable to prevent an Alert state from advancing, it will enter the Invasion state. A full Thargoid invasion force will enter the system, attacking starports and planetary ports in an effort to drive humanity out. Markets in an Invasion system will offer missions to destroy Thargoid vessels in an effort to prevent the aliens from taking full control. Other missions to bring supplies, recover human objects and evacuate refugees will also help the war effort.

Thargoid Control If a Thargoid invasion force is not driven out of a system in time, ports and planetary ports will continue to deteriorate due to sustained Thargoid assault. Eventually these locations will be abandoned, leaving the system in Thargoid control. Thargoid controlled space is highly dangerous, and no human presence remains to offer missions or support. The only way to regain control is to hunt down and destroy Thargoid ships in the system.

Thargoid Titan Thargoid Titans sit at the centre of a vast caustic cloud known as a Maelstrom. These gigantic ships are the epicentre of Thargoid forces invading human-occupied systems around its current location. Titan systems are considered extremely hazardous, and only the bravest of pilots with suitably outfitted ships should consider entering this space.
